item.title: REVIEW: Elegoo M1 Ultra review: A good first entry into the scanner market
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
The Elegoo M1 Ultra has a lot going for it, but it is not a standalone system. You’ll need to combine it with a powerful laptop to process the scanning data into anything useful. The good news it can be tethered via Wi-Fi. - -Needs a high end laptop for best results Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. The M1 Ultra is Elegoo’s first entry into the 3D scanner market. It is a feature-rich scanner with five scanning modes, four blue light laser modes, and a NIR binocular structured light mode. Most importantly, the scanner has a 3-in color touch screen and long battery life. It even includes a spare rechargeable battery, so you’re always prepared. The scanner can’t run without a fairly high end PC or Mac for processing power. It will need to be tethered to the laptop with a UBS-C cable or connected via Wi-Fi. I was able to get about five feet away from my subject in a harsh RF environment. I didn’t test it further than that, so it may go farther. The cable connection provides the fastest connectivity, making tethered scanning worth the hassle. The scanner’s output rivals any of the scanners I’ve tested, but it did require a little extra work to get there. At a current price of $1,599 at Elegoo, the M1 Ultra has features not found in other scanners at this price point. The Elegoo M1 Ultra comes with a nice hard case for travel, with a padded interior to protect the scanner, glass calibration board, spare battery, NIR filters, and a USB-C cable. Also included are a lens cleaning cloth and a packet of marker dots. Noticeably absent is a turntable for scanning smaller objects. (We borrowed a turntable from another scanner during this test.) The Elegoo M1 Ultra weighs 511g (1.12lbs) with its battery installed. It has a rubber grip below the screen and is nicely balanced. Users with large hands may find their thumbs blocking the screen. The onboard screen can be used to set the scanning parameters, start and stop scans, and monitor the scans as they progress. The 3-inch screen is small, but the UI is laid out perfectly. When setting parameters for a scan, the touch screen takes precedence over the tethered computer if you’re starting the scan from the scanner itself. The business end of the scanner has a series of blue, white, and infrared LEDs, blue lasers, and cameras. The included NIR filters are needed when scanning outdoors or in harsh light conditions. The battery and the spare can be charged using a USB-C cable when unmounted, and can be charged from the computer when operating the scanner in USB mode. The battery life is excellent. Almost all of our testing was done with one charge of the battery and its spare. Getting Started and Calibrating the Elegoo M1 Ultra Calibrating the Elegoo M1 Ultra is fairly easy given its light weight and the easy-to-follow software. Using the glass calibration board, the scanner is aimed at various angles and heights, following the directions on screen. The software shows an image of where the scanner should be and an image of the scanner as you move it. You have to match the two before moving on to the next spot. Scanner calibration can be a chore, but calibrating the M1 Ultra was simple. Installing the Software for Elegoo M1 Ultra Elegoo Scan can be downloaded from Elegoo’s website for Windows and Mac. The software works and looks like CrealityScan, which is a good thing since both make cleaning up individual scans and stitching multiple scans together fairly easy. The software does require a bunch of memory, with the more, the merrier. I tried running the software on an older PC laptop which met the minimum requirements, except it had only 8 GB of RAM, and it was not enough. Elegoo recommends a PC with Windows 10/11 (64-bit), an Intel Core i7 (13th Gen) or higher, an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 or higher (8 GB VRAM), and 32 GB or more of RAM. For Mac, they recommend macOS 14 or later, with an Apple M4 or later, and 32 GB or more of RAM. Minimum specs for both are 16gb of RAM, with Windows 10/11 (64-bit), Intel Core i7 (7th Gen), and an Nvidia GPU (6 GB VRAM) for PC, and macOS 14 or later, with an Apple M2 CPU. Blue Laser Line 3D Scanning with the Elegoo M1 Ultra The Elegoo M1 Ultra has 4 blue laser scanning modes: 34 crossed laser lines for quick scanning, 7 parallel lines for finer details, 1 line for scanning deeper, more difficult-to-capture holes, and markerless. The fewer the lines, the more time the scans take. I should point out that the turntable in the photo was borrowed from the Creality Pika Scanner, which we reviewed previously. One of my favorite use cases is scanning an item for import into a 3D printing project I am working on. I scanned a cheap 895 brushed motor commonly found in drills. The motor required several scans, and the M1 Ultra seemed to have trouble capturing the shinier parts of the object. Ultimately, I captured two scans that had enough data to be useful. The software has an automatic alignment tool which does a good job in most cases. In this case, it was baffled by the geometry. The manual alignment worked perfectly. Manual alignment requires adding markers matching points on both images. You do not have to be super exact with the placement. The software will smooth out any overlaps. Part of the mesh processing is hole filling. This also has an automatic and manual mode. Since the automatic mode was going to fill in the screw holes and cooling holes, I had to fill in the holes manually by clicking on them. This is a little tedious, but it worked well. After hole filling, smoothing, and simplifying, I was able to export the file as an STL and open it in Tinkercad. The size, and hole alignment were perfect for integrating the motor into a project. This bust of Michelangelo’s David came with an early Creality scanner and has become my main test file. It took three scans for me to get a good model, which was a recurring theme with the Elegoo M1 Ultra. Fortunately in this case, the auto alignment function worked perfectly. Even with multiple scans, there were still a few holes to fill. One of these can be seen in the finished model in the smooth, flat area above David’s left ear. Overall, the model generated is one of the best I’ve seen, and it printed extremely well once exported. The flaw at the bottom of the print was a bed adhesion issue rather than a problem with the model. NIR 3D Scanning with the Elegoo M1 Ultra Since I could not find a willing human victim…I mean, subject…to scan, I tried using the NIR mode to scan Clyde, our family’s favorite stuffed Clydesdale. This is a cautionary tale because 3D scanners in general have a tough time scanning black objects, as they absorb light rather than reflecting it. The scans weren’t bad, but they did leave big holes where the mane and tail were too dark to read. I was able to do a much better scan of Ali the Alligator. In NIR mode, the scanner is capable of 30fps. Even with the slower frame rate, the scanner was able to quickly capture Ali in two scans, without a ton of multiple passes. Each time you go over the same spot on an object, it’s possible to generate garbage data that has to be removed in the meshing process. The two scans align together automatically, and the finished model is pretty darn good. The scanner does feature color texture mapping. Other than the mouth, where a large hole needed to be filled, the color mapping was spot on. The Elegoo M1 Ultra is a good scanner that has a good feature set for the price. The light weight, onboard screen, long battery life, and stable Wi-Fi connection make it a joy to use. The ElegooScan software is fairly intuitive. It makes calibrating the scanner and turning the raw scans into usable models fairly easy. The Elegoo M1 Ultra did require multiple scans to get good coverage of objects, while other scanners I’ve tested could do it in one pass. The added complexity takes up a good deal of time and requires a fair amount of computer power, especially when cleaning up and aligning multiple scans. ElegooScan has the tools to make it work. Even with a pretty good model, you’ll likely also need a CAD program or other design tools to make the best use of the scans. If you’d like to save a few bucks and get a still excellent scanner, check out the Creality Pika, which is currently $699. If you want a scanner with a little more horsepower, check out the Creality Sermoon S1, which retails for $2,069. Creality also makes the Sermoon P1, which can run completely untethered and retails for $3,299.

item.title: SALES: The most comfortable bras to wear on travel days, tested by the editors of Condé Nast Traveller
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
If you’ve ever found yourself trying to get comfy on a long haul flight only to find it impossible because of a rogue underwire sticking into your ribs, you’ll already appreciate the importance of comfortable bras for travellers. Kitting yourself out with soft, supportive, and ideally non-wired undergarments before you head off on a trip is not a luxury, it’s essential. But don’t worry, comfortable bras don’t have to be frumpy. There are many underwear brands out there that have now recognised and addressed the bra needs of women all over the world, meaning you can get beautiful looking underwear that fits perfectly with your stylish in-flight loungewear choices. Simple, soft, comfortable and recycled – there’s so much to love about the Nudea bras. Despite being non-wired, these are very supportive even for larger busts and they can be styled to wear under almost anything thanks to the multi-way straps. You can choose this style in different materials too, from organic cotton to a microfibre stretch fabric made out of 86 per cent recycled polyamide. Our testers found these bras to be a dream travel companion and loved the look, particularly the light, neutral shades, which are perfect for wearing under a white shirt or dress on holiday. As an added bonus, every purchase comes with a free laundry bag to help you take good care of your new favourite bra when it goes through the wash. We love the seamless design in the Stripe & Stare range, all of which had a ‘second skin’ feel as they were so deliciously soft and lightweight. There are many beautiful colours to choose from here, in each of the variety of styles. You’ll be able to find differing levels of support and comfort for a range of bust sizes, with our favourites being the Triangle and Smooth Sculpt shapes. The latter has a smoothing and contouring effect that’s great for wearing under a t-shirt, along a thicker bottom band that helps add support for those with a fuller bust. The barely-there triangle bra is the one to reach for if you want that bra-free feel without actually going braless, prettied up with the addition of a flash of lace at the bottom. Cool French label Ysé Paris was founded in 2021. It’s now won B Corp status for its stellar commitment to creating sustainable pieces in that easy-chic feminine style that Parisians do so well. Predictably, the lingerie is delicate and gorgeous. While this seamless bra isn’t as pretty as the brand’s lacy pieces, it’s a stellar option for flight days, crafted using a seamless knitting technique in ultra-soft ribbed microfibre that slips over your head, so there’s no rigid fastenings to dig in during long-haul flights. The lightweight triangle cut makes for a natural, unrestrictive fit – exactly what we all need in an economy seat – and it will also work nicely under loose linen shirts and slouchy knitwear when you’re off the plane. Finding a bra or a bralette that balances cloud-like comfort with actual support isn’t easy, but Lounge has done a very good job, and at a pleasingly keen price point. This mostly comes down to the spacer fabric moulded cups, which are made from a 3D-knitted material that uses microscopic air pockets instead of dense foam. It makes for a feather-light, breathable and crush-resistant shape (good for squishing into your carry-on), and ensures a smooth finish under a T-shirt and medium support without extra bulk. It also gives a slight push-up effect, which is impressive for a wire-free bra. There’s a wider elastic underband and relatively wide straps to keep everything securely in place, and a padded hook-and-eye closure to ward off irritation when leaning against an aeroplane seat. Our top pick for travel days? The softskin bandeau by shapewear brand Heist. Not only is this a good item to pack for holidays in hotter climes to wear under a strappy (or strapless) dress, but it’s extraordinarily soft and supple with a barely there feel, as the name suggests. It even has an aloe vera finish to be extra kind to skin. To be clear, this isn’t a supportive bra by any stretch of the imagination, but it is extraordinarily comfy. It’s genuinely as close to being braless as is possible, so bear that in mind. Nonetheless, if you want to feel some coverage without any kind of compression or restriction, go for this. If you want the smooth, sculpted shape of a traditional T-shirt bra without any wire-induced discomfort, Triumph’s Body Make-Up Soft Touch is a solid option. It’s made from velvet-soft jersey fabric with ultra-light foam cups, that adds subtle definition that feels weightless when on. It has a comfy extra-wide band and a totally seamless finish, to help ensure zero digging and an invisible finish under thin tops and travel tees. You’ve probably seen Lemonade Dolls adverts circulating on social media. They’ve gone all out with their campaign, but have racked up a huge number of loyal customers because they produce bras that deliver on both comfort and style. They may be one of the more reasonably-priced on the list, but these bras stand up against expensive alternatives. They look gorgeous, with lace or smooth styles, and there’s now a plunge bra, too, in sizes all the way up to H cup and band sizes ranging from 30-44. There’s a ‘high support’ range, designed with a ‘magic triangle cross section’ for large breasts, again all completely wire-free. Part of the range is made from 95 per cent biodegradable fibres, and the brand donates underwear (and funds) to women in refugee centres and camps all over Europe. Understatement’s fun and feminine selection of bras is happily travel-friendly in all the best ways, with so many styles to choose from here, each as pretty as the last. It shows that just because your in-flight underwear isn’t on show, you can still treat yourself – especially if it’s comfortable. The little details make things all the better: the labels are made from soft silicone (no itchy tags here!), with a non-wired design offering support without restriction, plus satin-covered elastic underbands for an extra level of comfort and indulgence. The Fits Everybody range of bras from Skims – Kim Kardashian's line of basics and shapewear – has expanded. It now comes in nine different shapes to suit different bust sizes and needs for every eventuality and event, including everyday bras, push-up bras and strapless options. Our editors love the t-shirt bra for flight days. It has a lightweight feel, smooth shape, non-wired design and buttery soft fabric. Say what you will about the reality star, but one thing’s for sure – she knows how to create a comfortable bra. If you’ve been waiting for a brand on this list that offers bras with underwires and full coverage, Copenhagen-based brand Organic Basics, has everything you need, along with a solid range of non-underwired bralettes – which are naturally our pick for flight days. We love the supersoft organic cotton fabric, which is pillowy soft and environmentally friendly. As is the Copenhagen way, this brand creates all products only from recycled, recyclable, plant-based and organic materials, paired with ethical means of production. Although we were looking for comfort over allure, Traveller editors were delighted to discover that there are many non-wired bras out there that also give a great confidence boost. Women of all cup sizes and ages tested a wide variety of bras over multiple days, specifically looking for something that delivered a complete trifecta of supportiveness, style and comfort. Below are their top picks for travel (and everyday use). You’ll never want to wear an underwired bra again. As a travel and commerce writer for Condé Nast Traveller for the last three years, plus a further four-year stint writing shopping guides for Good Housekeeping, I have tested hundreds of products – so I know how to find the best of the best. I spend a large portion of my time living out of a suitcase, trialling gear on the move – I tend to take at least one flight a month. It means my recommendations are grounded in hands-on experience, with most products tried out over a considerable length of time. For further recommendations, explore our other guides:

item.title: REVIEW: Aomei Backupper Professional 8.5 review: Local and online backup, with ransomware protection
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
- File backup, sync, and imaging in one program - Affordable online storage (for backup and restore only) - Doesn’t support third-party online storage services - Doesn’t let you create new folders when defining a backup destination - Boot disk creation remains problematic With online storage and malware protection, Aomei Backupper 8.5 can now compete with the likes of Acronis True Image in the backup, sync, and disaster recovery category. If only it would fix a couple niggling issues. This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Prices Today: Aomei Backupper Professional I last reviewed Aomei Backupper’s imaging, file backup, and sync program at version 7 when it added proprietary, but extremely affordable cloud backup to the mix. There were a couple interface snags and recalcitrant but fixable boot media, yet it remained a worthy backup suite. Version 8.5 of Aomei Backupper Professional adds anti-ransomware and a lighter-hued, friendlier-looking interface to the mix. The program also proved fast and reliable in nearly all aspects of testing. Alas, interface foibles and malformed recovery boot media still beset the program’s quest for 4.5 stars — two years after I first reported them. Maybe next time. Read on to learn more, then see our roundup of the best Windows backup software for comparison. What are Aomei Backupper Professional 8.5’s features? Backupper Pro’s features run the gamut of backup functionality: imaging of your files/folders, system, drives, and partitions; dedicated email and Outlook backup; Windows PE disaster recovery boot media; system/disk/partition cloning; a recovery partition (boot environment); and several flavors of folder sync. Backups and syncs may be saved anywhere, to any type of non-optical media (optical is supported for boot discs), including network locations, which may also be included in backups. You can schedule backups as granularly as one hour (continuous is available as real-time sync), as well as run pre- and post-backup commands, including scripts. Beyond that, Aomei’s changelog lists mostly smaller improvements and optimizations. All welcome, but nothing particularly noteworthy other than the aforementioned ransomware protection (see below). Backupper’s new Ransomware Protection basically runs in the background and locks files to prevent them from being encrypted then deleted (which is the way most ransomware works). Backupper also includes a number of storage-related utilities, including a disk-wipe app that will overwrite sensitive data, destroy malware, etc; an image explorer so you can browse files on images; an image integrity checker; and a hidden emergency partition containing a recovery copy of your Windows installation (one-key recovery), as you’ll find on large vendors’ PCs. Mirroring maintains an exact duplicate of the source folder’s contents in the destination folder, including removing files deleted from the source folder. Two-way sync simply means that changes made in either the source or destination folder are duplicated in the other. Real-time sync is just what is sounds like: instantaneous mirroring of changes made in the source folder to the destination, rather than by scheduling. How easy is Aomei Backupper Professional to use? Aomei Backupper is similar in both appearance and workflow to Acronis True Image, especially with the now lighter color scheme. Both feature a column of categories on the left, with a pane of sub-categories to the right that morph into detail view. The GUI is clean, friendly, and the features are explained with easily understandable language. That said, choosing destination locations could be easier. The program still doesn’t allow you to select a network location using the mouse. You must type in the IP address, e.g., \192.168.1.105\Public, though once you’re at the parent location a normal browser tree pops up. Huh? Another annoyance is the inability to create a new folder when browsing to select a destination. For instance, if you browse to a folder named “Backups” there’s no way to create a subfolder named “Aomei.” You must use Windows Explorer to handle this chore. These are piddling details that are easy to fix, and I wholly expected them to have been addressed in the two years since I last visited the program. The fact that they haven’t been makes me wonder if anyone at the company actually uses their own product. Of course, the free version, which is what most people will start off with, suffers a perpetual upgrade nag on the main screen, as well as other nudges to buy it. If you like the software, you should probably support the company that provided it. How much is Aomei Backupper Professional 8.5? The pricing of Backupper Professional is a more complicated topic than with many other products — the prices vary depending on where you see them. Thanks for that. The prices shown below are what you see if you hit the buy button inside the trial version. I saw no cloud storage when simply browsing to the Backupper web page normally. Backupper Professional is available for $39.95 annually (often on sale), which bumps up to $59.95 if you add Aomei Cloud with 1TB of storage. As of October 31, 2026, this was discounted to $49.95. A perpetual license is $69.95 for one user, or $89.95 for five users, but this doesn’t include cloud storage. Aomei offers this to perpetual users at $20 a year according to media relations, or $30 according to tech support last time I talked to them. Either way, $20 or $30, it’s quite a bargain, though it can only be used in conjunction with Backupper to back up and restore files. Most services are multiples of those prices, which ameliorates my wish that Backupper Professional supported third-party online storage as well. It doesn’t. There are also small business plans: Workstation for $50 yearly with PXE boot ($60 with the 1TB of online storage), Server for $150 with support for various Windows server operating systems. Additionally, two enterprise-oriented versions are available: Technician for $499, and Technician Plus for $699 with image deployment and the portable version. While many of the advanced features discussed above are available only in the Professional and Enterprise versions of Backupper, many users will be just fine with the basic set available in the free Standard version. There’s a version comparison here if you want the complete lowdown. How does Aomei Backupper Professional 8.5 perform? The Windows version of Backupper Professional performed both quickly and without error this time around in nearly every task. Imaging, file backup, and sync to both local, network, and online proceeded apace given the bandwidth available on each medium. Alas, the Windows PE recovery thumb drive that Backupper Professional created was not recognized as bootable — a long-running issue with the program. Using the free Rufus 4.8 boot disk creator to write the Backupper ISO to a thumb drive created a disk that would boot. However, that was only if I lowered the BIOS boot security settings — the UEFI used in the ISO had been deprecated. Put bluntly, for disaster recovery to work, you need a bootable disk and creating one with Backupper Pro requires jumping through hoops that many less experienced users might not even know exist. Overall, Backupper is a very good performer and super reliable with most tasks — but, geez, Aomei, fix the darn boot media! Should you buy Aomei Backupper Professional 8.5? Imaging, file backup, and disaster recovery for $40 with 1TB of online storage for $10 to $30 a year more is a fantastic bargain, even if the latter is only usable for Backupper backup and restore. Overall, the suite if very competent. However, Aomei’s continuing lack of attention to fine details, and the recovery-media creation issues again cost it half a star. A half a star I was inclined to add in light of the addition of malware protection and the lighter-colored interface. Note that you can use any backup software, including the free Backupper Standard, with nearly any online storage service these days thanks to cloud storage managers.

item.title: REVIEW: Marshall Stanmore IV Review: Plenty of Punch, If Not Quite Enough Polish
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Marshall has spent over a decade in home audio, diversifying its offerings well beyond professional sound equipment. The Stanmore IV ($429), as the name suggests, is just one more entry in a series of home speakers built with classic Marshall aesthetics, such as the slightly smaller Middleton II ($329). The Stanmore IV improves on the Stanmore III with better Bluetooth codec support, more concealed port placement, and more extensive EQ adjustments in the app. It makes for an exciting little home speaker with some crisp detail at the high end. Although stylish and perhaps too iconic to pass up for Marshall fans, it's pricey for what it offers. It swims in the waters between portable party speakers and proper bookshelf speakers without quite achieving the best of either. Ultimately, the Stanmore IV can’t outdo our Editors' Choice picks, the boombox-style Sony ULT Field 7 ($499.99) and the audiophile-friendly Fluance Ri71 ($499.99). Meanwhile, the Fender Elie 12 ($399) also delivers powerful sound and vintage amplifier styling in a similar form factor, but with greater flexibility and a lower price. More than 12 years on from the introduction of the first Marshall Stanmore speaker, you’d be excused for thinking the new Stanmore IV was the original. It bears a strikingly similar design, continuing to offer a leatherette-wrapped box with a woven front cover vis-à-vis Marshall’s famous speaker cabinets, though Marshall also offers a cream color scheme here. At 7.99 by 13.78 by 7.28 inches (HWD) and 8.98 pounds, it’s not the same size or weight as predecessors (proving a bit lighter, in fact), but it’s close. The Stanmore IV includes classic amplifier-style dials on the top for overall volume, bass, and treble. Rather than hard limits, these dials include LED indicator lights to show how high they're set. Beyond these, you get a button for cycling through input sources, with lights indicating Bluetooth, AUX, and RCA inputs. There’s a jog control that lets you play or pause audio with a press, and skip backward or forward with left and right flicks, respectively. There’s also a large physical power switch; awkwardly, there is no indication of which direction it needs to flip to power on. Thankfully, the many LED indicators on the top of the speaker help make it clear when the speaker is on or off. Most of that was present in the prior edition. This generation introduces a Marshall M Button with special functions you can adjust in the app, but it’s not a great selling point. The bigger updates this generation are a little harder to see. The Stanmore IV has more powerful amplification, with a 60W class-D amplifier for the five-inch woofer and two 25W class-D amplifiers for the 0.75-inch tweeters. The tweeters have new waveguides to help disperse the sound more evenly, since they don’t have any way to angle them for optimal dispersion. Marshall has also curved the exit to the bass reflex port and moved it back to the bottom of the speaker, where it had been on the first-gen Stanmore. Perhaps more critically, the Marshall Stanmore IV steps up its wireless connectivity. The Stanmore III launched in 2022 and had Bluetooth 5.2 with support only for the SBC codec. The Stanmore IV steps that up to Bluetooth 6.0 and supports the AAC, LDAC, and LC3 codecs. That’s a huge gain for wireless audio quality and beats out the Sonos Era 300 in codec support—though the latter offers Wi-Fi streaming, better audio, and more setup flexibility. The speaker also supports Bluetooth Multipoint. In addition to Bluetooth, the speaker has a 3.5mm AUX port on the top for convenient access and stereo RCA ports on the bottom for hidden, longer-term connections. Marshall has integrated Auracast support as well, though not in the simplest way, nor with an open ecosystem. There's no way to use the Stanmore IV as an Auracast broadcast host, nor a quick way to run it as a receiver. Using another speaker I had on hand as an Auracast source (the much cheaper Tribit Stormbox Max), I could quickly connect another Auracast-capable device (the EarFun Wave Pro X) to the broadcast, but the Stanmore IV would not connect. The speaker can connect to the $299 Marshall Heddon hub and then be linked with other speakers. Unfortunately, this means getting a stereo set is a lot more costly than just buying two Stanmore IV units. Marshall says it plans to add support for Auracast linking in its app, but it was not available at the time of testing. Though it looks like a sizable party speaker, the Stanmore IV still isn’t portable. It has no built-in battery and needs wall power supplied through a port on the underside. That at least keeps it looking clean if it’s not tucked next to a wall. It also isn't waterproof. If you need a portable speaker that can also get wet, the Sony ULT Field 7 is a better option. It will even let you plug in a guitar or microphone. The Stanmore IV works with the Marshall app, which is confusingly different from the Marshall Bluetooth app that supports some of Marshall’s other speakers and even recent headphones like the Milton ANC. The app will prompt you to create an account during setup, but it is not required to use the app. Up front, the app provides volume and input selection options. It also offers a few adjustable settings. You get a decent five-band EQ you can customize, plus a few presets for simple boosts or cuts to treble and bass. It also has a few quick acoustic compensations you can select to help with room dynamics, adjusting the sound if the speaker is placed close to the edge of a table or shelf, a wall, a corner, or a combination of the three. The speaker includes a special M Button that, by default, attempts to launch Spotify Tap and play Spotify music. It can also be set to cycle between EQ presets or do nothing. The app will also let you adjust the brightness of LED indicators and set how quickly the speakers enter standby mode after no audio has been playing for a set period. With very limited capabilities, it's not the most exciting feature to have on board. The Stanmore IV is a powerful speaker with a party-ready sound, thanks to impressively strong bass that digs down to about 40Hz before dropping off. It delivers clean mids and crisp detail in the high end, but, as is expected from a single-speaker design, its stereo imaging isn’t very wide. It ends up providing subtle textures, and for energetic listening, it can prove a good pairing. Even the strong bass isn’t perfect, though. At just 50% volume, the speaker already distorts slightly while playing the opening bass triplets to The Knife’s “Silent Shout,” though not on every note. It’s worse at full volume. The speaker holds up better when handling more, as the distortion subsides when other track elements layer on top of the bass triplets. The speaker digs deep, hitting the sub-bass quarter notes well, though they aren’t entirely full-sounding and they slacken as the notes glissando to lower frequencies. The mids and treble bite hard, giving the synth melody its full ferocity and texture. The open hi-hat has lovely brilliance, but the closed hi-hat rings a bit too much. The speaker also provides a fairly congested soundstage. Some of the stereo effects come through, like the vocal harmony phasing, but it’s not very clear, and the vocals are a bit flat. The upper harmony ends up hard to hear through the track. Pad hits throughout the song, which tend to have a long tail of reverb, also vanish too quickly. Kendrick Lamar’s “Loyalty” continues to exhibit that high-frequency ringing from the cymbals, which gives the speaker a bit of high-end harshness. That’s easily dialed off with a slight turn of the treble dial, though. The bass powers through quite impressively. The first chorus introduces a recurring sub-bass line that can be incredibly hard for speakers to dig down into, but the Stanmore IV actually manages to bump out all but the lowest note with considerable force, giving it plenty of punch for parties. The highest note in this line is a bit boosted next to the rest, but doesn’t sound terrible. Lamar’s and Rihanna’s vocals come through clearly with clean mids. Bill Callahan’s “Drover” helps reveal where the Stanmore IV is doing a little too much. The bass power of the Stanmore IV is plainly overemphasizing what it gets, as the constant patter of the kick drum beats out over the track rather than underlining it. Callahan’s baritone vocals get a pleasing fullness at least. The rhythm guitar, electric guitar, fiddle, and cymbals benefit from the speaker's presence and brilliance, though they can still ring a bit. Because of the narrow soundstage, the instruments don’t get much room to stand out. This congested soundstage makes the Stanmore IV a rather poor match for orchestral music, such as John Adams’ The Gospel According to the Other Mary. During the opening track, the orchestra’s range might be well recreated by the speaker, but it becomes claustrophobic. The bass and choir also become noise, muddling the rest of the performance. During solo or duo passages, the performance is better, but as more instruments pile on, it gets to be more wall-of-sound than anything. The speaker’s Bluetooth latency is low enough to work OK with video. There’s a small amount of delay, but it’s short enough that your brain will likely adapt quickly enough. And for pure audio listening, it's a non-factor. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Marshall Stanmore IV delivers punchy bass and crisp treble, which do a lot for the listening experience, and the iconic design and brand will probably help it sell quite well. But at $429, it’s not quite as capable as a speaker ought to be. Its narrow soundstage can't compete with the brilliance of separate bookshelf speakers like the Fluance Ri71; it’s not as flexible as the Fender Elie 12, which adds portability and a nifty guitar input while remaining attractive; and for parties, the Sony ULT Field 7 can play louder and is more portable than the JBL, if less stylish. Even so, the Stanmore IV might win a place in your heart with its iconic looks, intuitive amp-like controls, and exciting audio signature. I have reviewed hundreds of products with a particular emphasis on computers and the broad field of peripherals, especially audio gear. item.title: REVIEW: Oukitel WP63 rugged phone review
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
As a smartphone, the WP63 has little to write home about, aside from a substantial battery and a curious, intentional ability to start a conflagration. Smokers and pyromaniacs will love this device, but it's not the most practical design Oukitel has launched - -Heavy to carry and difficult to pocket Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. Oukitel has a strange approach to phone naming: they release phones in seemingly random order. Therefore, the WP66 has been around for a while, and now the WP63 has arrived. But perhaps the problem isn’t the order in which these devices were announced, but when they actually get delivered. With so many phones on Oukitel’s stable, you might be wondering, not unreasonably, what makes this one different? On the surface, this is a heavy rugged design where battery capacity is paramount, mostly at the expense of fitting in a normal-sized pocket. That hints it's aimed at the adventure market, since this phone could easily last a week without a charge, if you use it wisely. Reinforcing that notion, it also has a big speaker and a camping light. But one feature on this phone I’ve never seen before sounds a little bonkers. This is the first phone I’ve reviewed that has an ‘ignitor’ in it. Yes, something to intentionally start fires, not just accidentally. If you need to start fires, or you just can’t give up smoking, then the WP63 might be the perfect phone for you. In other respects, this isn’t an especially powerful smartphone, but it can reverse charge at 18W using an inbuilt USB-C cable, and it is running Android 16. It’s also not expensive, making it a good candidate if the rugged requirement is only for a specific trip or job. However, I can’t see myself putting this in our best rugged phone collection, even with its unique features. - When is it out? Available from Oukitel in early November - Where can you get it? Only from Oukitel While I was writing this review, I was slightly confused by the lack of a web page for this device, since I knew its release was imminent. Thankfully, now the WP63 has a webpage, and I’ve been promised it should be available to purchase by the time you read this review. The quoted US price is $389.99, supposedly 35% less than the $599.99 MSRP Oukitel imagined when they cooked up this phone. UK customers pay £294.58, and in the EU it’s €348.05. But keep in mind that prices can change. Unusually for a Chinese phone maker, these prices are roughly identical based on the current exchange rates between the US dollar, British pound, and Euro. While the WP63 has some unique features, plenty of rugged designs offer 20000 mAh of battery capacity, but most pack more processing power than this model. A phone with a similar spec is the Blackview XPLORE 1, which costs $359.99 on Amazon.com, and at that price you do get more RAM and 55W charging. That pricing suggests the WP63 isn’t a bargain, but if it saves you from carrying another ignition source, the cost difference may be worth it. The WP63 isn’t an expensive phone, but it also has modest specs. If I were inclined to hike a long way, maybe over several days, I’m not sure I’d take the WP63 along. At 629g and an awkward fit in most pockets, this is a hefty device that you wouldn’t want to carry in open water. However, Oukitel sloped the undersides, so it’s relatively easy to handle unless you have weak wrists. Button placement is typical, with the power and volume rocker on the right and a PTT custom button on the left with the SIM slot. One mild annoyance was that when it wants a fingerprint for access, it places a fingerprint icon on the screen, where some phones have the sensor embedded under the display. This isn't one of those phones, and the fingerprint reader is actually on the power button. That said, most people should be able to transition to this device easily. On the rear is a 3W speaker for summoning beach-party people, and that pushes the two rear cameras out to the edge of the phone. What space is left by the speaker and camera cluster is taken up with a substantial camping LED, one of those that can temporarily blind you if set to full brightness and looked at. This device has no wireless charging because there is no open space for it. None of this is especially unusual, as I’ve seen a dozen or more rugged phones with a big lamp and speaker, probably in the past year. Where the WP63 goes off into uncharted territory is with two other special functions, one of which is a short but integrated USB-C cable. This cable can be used to charge and also reverse charge other devices, making it unnecessary to carry a charging cable with you. I like this idea, and even with the shortness of the cable, it's useful. The other special feature is slightly more controversial, because the WP63 can set things on fire, hopefully when you intend for it to do so. Given how phones and other battery-powered devices are often blamed for starting fires, it seems contradictory to actually design a phone specifically to set things on fire, but Oukitel did. Along the top edge is the ignitor, which comes out of a tube when pressed down and sideways, so it doesn’t deploy accidentally. A phone app controls when it heats and for how long, so it should be impossible for this to happen unintentionally. The minimum heating time is four seconds, the maximum is ten, and then there is a longer period during which the ignitor must cool down before it can be fired again. You are advised that the ignitor gets extremely hot, and it is best not to touch it when in use. So what is this practically useful for? Well, I suspect it's fine for lighting cigarettes, the odd firework, but you would need some paper or dry tinder to start a campfire using it. The box includes a spare igniter element, so it will eventually burn through the heated wire it uses, and you can replace that part. Some grease is also provided to make sure the igniter deploys smoothly when you want it. I don’t know how much power this feature uses, but it will have an impact if you use it repeatedly. As a non-smoker and non-pyromaniac, this isn’t a feature I’d find much use for, but I accept that others might find it useful. I just wouldn’t want to be found with this phone in an era which has had an unexplained forest fire recently. The UNISOC T8200 (UMS9621S) is a mid-range 5G chip. It has eight cores in two clusters, with two Cortex-A76 cores at up to 2.3GHz and six smaller cores at up to 2.1GHz. A two-core Mali G57 handles graphics, and the chip is built on TSMC’s older 6nm process. That process is a little dated now, but it remains perfectly efficient if underwhelming. Memory support is sensible. The controller handles LPDDR4 and LPDDR4X, with the latter used here. That means no speedy LPDDR5, which holds back peak performance. The integrated modem covers sub-6 GHz 5G with carrier aggregation. There is no mmWave here, but few phones at this level need it. The camera and display features are generous for the price. UNISOC says the chip supports sensors up to 108MP, 4K video recording and a 120Hz FHD+ display. Variable refresh rate support should also help battery life. However, not all of those features apply to this phone. So how does it perform? Day to day, it should feel fine. Scrolling, browsing, social media and video streaming sit well within its abilities. The two A76 cores give it a useful turn of speed when apps need it. Notebookcheck lists a Geekbench 6 single-core score of around 750. That is respectable, and clearly better than entry-level silicon. Gaming is where limits appear. Two GPU cores will manage casual titles and older 3D games without fuss. Demanding modern games will need lower settings and will not hold high frame rates for long. I would not buy it for that job. Against the competition, it sits below chips like the Dimensity 8100, which uses a 4nm process and much faster Cortex A78 cores. It is a budget-friendly alternative, not a rival, and Oukitel only use UFS 2.2 storage because it works in this context. The allocation of 256GB is plenty for most people, and you can add a 1TB microSD if you need to capture lots of video. For a rugged or value-focused handset, the T8200 is a sound choice. It is quick enough, frugal enough and well connected. Just keep expectations realistic. The one area where Oukitel pushed the boat out is battery capacity, with 20000mAh to splurge. That obviously provides a substantial running time, but it can also be used through reverse charging to keep other devices powered. One nice note about that feature is that if it is charging another phone, for example, and the battery capacity hits 20%, it will stop so it doesn’t exhaust the battery entirely. The Oukitel WP63 has three cameras: Rear cameras: 64MP Omnivision OV64B40 , 8MP Hynix Hi-846 (Night Vision) The camera sensor collection on this phone isn’t the best, but it isn’t junk either. I’ve seen the 64MP Omnivision OV64B40 on many devices, and it performs decently on most of them, even if it’s not a sensor a premium phone would use. The biggest issue is that it has no optical zoom, so all zoom is digital. That undermines the premise of using a 64MP sensor with pixel binning to deliver 16MP images that are sharp and perfectly saturated. The results without zooming are therefore much better than those with. I took some decent pictures using this sensor, but it does like plenty of light. One positive aspect of this sensor is that it will capture 4K video, but only at 30 fps. In fact, it's locked to 30 fps at all resolutions unless you use ‘slow motion’ mode, where the frame rate jumps to 120 fps for 1080p or 720p capture. The second rear sensor is an 8MP Hynix Hi-846 Night Vision chip. An SK Hynix part with an 8-megapixel 1/4-inch sensor and 1.12 µm pixels. It outputs 3264x2448 natively, so the resolution in your screenshot matches its true array and not a cropped one. Works well if the subject is close enough to be illuminated by the IR array, The front-facing 20MP Sony IMX376 seems ideal for selfies, but it is limited to 1080p video. And, as I always check, this phone is rated for Widevine L1 encryption, so streamed video can be higher than 480p. However, the screen resolution isn't enough for 1080p streaming, so it's not a huge benefit. Overall, the cameras can take decent photos and video, but these choices seem mostly budget-driven and not meant to deliver photographic excellence. To be direct, if I put this phone up against one of the many Dimensity 8200 phones, it would look like it was going backwards. So instead, I chose the UleFone RugKing 5 Pro, another relatively low-power handset that also uses a Unisoc SoC. The T8200 appears to have about 50% more power than the T7250 from a compute perspective, and the G57 MP2 is double the performance of its base counterpart. Neither phone would excite anyone who likes to game, but the WP63 beats the RugKing 5 Pro in all but one area. That’s the flipside of powerful phones, in that delivering that performance consumes more power. Here, the extra performance of the WP63 comes at a cost of battery life. Although being able to run PCMark for nearly 30 hours and still have 14% of the capacity left is an accomplishment that many phones would be envious. One major issue I ran into with the review hardware was that the provided charger refused to charge the phone, even with the cable that Oukitel provided. That should not be a problem, since I have plenty of USB-C chargers. Except when I used one of my 100W-capable chargers, it peaked at 20W while charging the phone, which meant after 30 minutes it had only recovered 16% of its power. That said, even if it accepted the full 33W, I calculate it would still take four hours to recharge the WP63, and possibly longer. So this isn’t a phone you want to wake up next to after forgetting to charge it. Overall, the WP63 is power-efficient enough to deliver a reasonable user experience and run most Android apps, but it's hardly rocket-powered. What an odd phone. If we ignore the slightly charred elephant in this room, this is a mid-order rugged phone with plenty of battery capacity to keep it alive for a decent number of days away from civilisation. The cameras can take acceptable photos and video, and the asking price isn’t excessive. This is something you could say about a dozen or more other designs. But people won’t be buying this phone for only those features, will they? No, they’ll want the phone that can light a cigarette, or fireworks, or burn down half of Canada. Part of me thinks this wasn’t a great idea, but it’s possible to create a fire with a glass bottle, a magnifying glass, or a battery and two wires, so am I overreacting? Possibly. My concern is that, since this is a phone and can be remotely controlled, someone might use it to initiate something remotely. But then phones have been used to do that without having an ignitor in them, so perhaps the truly dangerous part is the phone? Whatever the answer is, because I’m far from being an expert, the WP63 does have a feature that no other phone I’ve seen sports. Will it spawn a whole new generation of fire-starting phones? I doubt it. But if you need to carry something that can start a fire in a pinch, the WP63 exists. Should I buy a Oukitel WP63? Buy it if... While 20000 mAh isn’t the biggest phone battery I’ve seen, it’s a good size, and if managed, it will last a long time. The only caveat to this capacity is that the maximum charging wattage is only 33W, which means even if you can get the provided charger to work, it won’t be charging that quickly. Something I never thought I’d write in a review is that this phone is perfect for setting fire to things, assuming they burn. Chain-smokers, firework fans and common or garden-variety pyromaniacs will love the WP63 and its inclusive gift from the gods. Don't buy it if... If weight and size matter to you, then give this a miss. At 629g and 27mm deep, this is not an easily pocketable device by any definition. There is an argument that with this phone you won’t need a power pack for other devices, a charging cable or a lighter, but it's still heavy. item.title: SALES: Eufy's clever outdoor security camera that lives inside is now available to buy
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Eufy's clever outdoor security camera that lives inside is now available to buy The $80 Window Camera E10 sticks to your window, pointed outwards. Outdoor security cameras are a useful addition to any home, but not everyone is able to install one, be that for practical or rental reasons. Or maybe they just don't need the hassle of picking up a drill and hoping the holes end up where they're supposed to. Anker has a workaround for all these issues thanks to sub-brand Eufy's Window Camera E10, which is now available to buy in the US. First announced back at IFA in the summer, it's actually an indoor camera that you stick to your window, with the lens facing outwards. As well as its completely tool-free installation (the camera sticks to your window via a residue-free adhesive), the Window Camera E10 features a manually adjustable 25-degree downward tilt mechanism that allows you to set the best angle for whatever you have it monitoring. It has a 2.5k resolution, up to 8x digital zoom, and MaxColor Night Vision for after-dark recording. Footage is saved to an SD card up to 256GB in size, but you'll have to add that yourself as you don't get one in the box. As glass reflects light, recording the outside of your house from inside often presents a number of issues, but Anker thinks it's solved the problem with a lens that's flush to the window, preventing background light from reaching it in the same way. The company says that clear glass windows with one or two panes work best. If your windows are particularly thick, Anker warns that reflections from the extra layers may result in glare if you have lamps on. Frosted or patterned glass is obviously a no-no too. And if you live in an apartment on a high floor, the E10 probably isn't the device for you either, as there will likely be significant blind spots in the frame. There is a built-in microphone too, which picks up ambient noise and anything loud directly outside. However, Anker warns that the reliability of the audio will depend a lot on glass thickness. The Window Camera E10 supports dual-band 2.4Ghz and 5Ghz Wi-Fi and can record 24/7. AI human, pet and vehicle recognition is built in and does not require a subscription if you just rely on local storage. If there's a potential snag, depending on your home layout, it's that you need to connect the camera to power via a single USB-C cable. Most indoor cameras can easily be positioned near a power source, but not everyone will have one of those directly next to their window. There's no battery-powered option. The Eufy Window Camera E10 is available to buy now for $80.

item.title: REVIEW: This futuristic wearable exoskeleton makes me feel like RoboCop
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
I’ve had an exoskeleton under my desk for several months now. That’s not a sentence I ever expected to type, but 2026 is weird like that. It was sent to me by a company called Hypershell, and it’s quite the conversation starter. Even after owning it for this long, I’m still trying to figure out who this thing is for. We got wearable exoskeletons before GTA VI When I first heard that a company wanted to send over an “exoskeleton,” I immediately pictured the big loader mechs from Alien, but the reality is a bit more mundane. In the end, the Hypershell X Ultra S that I received (which is modeled here by my partner) ended up looking a lot more like man-meets-machine augment from Deus Ex. Rather than turning you into a truck on legs, the exoskeleton instead adds a bit of pep to your step. First, you have to unload it from its sturdy carrying case, adjust it to fit your waist (every time, using two lockable clips), and strap what I’ve come to think of as the “thrusters” to your thighs. This is a lot less hassle than it sounds. The device then sits predominantly on your hips like a padded hiking rucksack, with the swappable battery pack in the small of your back. It’s comfortable enough to wear for hours at a time, with around 18 miles (30 kilometers) of range or around 7.5 hours of walking from a single charge in the most power-efficient mode. In that power efficient mode the Hypershell provides a small boost to performance. It’s an odd sensation, but it feels a bit like someone is giving you an extra push as you walk. You can control the level of assistance using the button on the side of the unit, or using a mobile app. In addition to Eco mode, there’s a far more powerful Hyper mode that delivers considerably more assistance at the cost of battery life. It’s comical how much more powerful Hyper mode is. Rather than a gentle push, Hyper mode jolts you into action and is designed for vigorous exercise or anywhere you find yourself needing the additional help. The Hypershell X Ultra S that I’ve currently got strapped to me as I write this costs a cool $1,999, and that’s a price you’re going to want to mull over as you ask yourself… What do you do with it? Hypershell is very clear what it designed these exoskeletons for: active individuals who want to run, hike, and cycle in all terrains. The product description covers the full gamut, from trail running, to gravel cycling, hiking through the snow, coming down mountains with lots of weight strapped to your back, or simply walking along flat terrain with a gentle boost. I’ve tried all but the gnarliest of these activities, and I can say that it works. Hiking up hills with the Hypershell strapped to your waist is considerably easier, especially if you’re loaded up with supplies. Though the exoskeleton adds weight, the help you get while cycling more than makes up for it. I imagine if you were recovering from injury or found walking for extended periods difficult, a device like this would provide immediate support. I’m no elite athlete, though I consider myself fit and enthusiastic about exercise. I go to the gym four days out of the week, I do extras on the side like pilates and running, and I cycle as often as possible instead of driving. For me, a device like the Hypershell doesn’t make a lot of sense. I want that added challenge, it’s the reason I’m going the long way around when I hop on my bike. In that sense, you really need to know that you want a helping hand in order to drop a nice bike’s worth of money on this thing. You also need to be able to swallow your pride and not feel too self-conscious if you want to wear it in public. On a bike or a hiking trail, it’s not such a big deal. Walking through town is another matter, and you’re going to get some looks. My favorite mode isn’t an augment at all Funnily enough, the most use I have gotten out of the Hypershell X so far has been in the experimental Fitness mode. Rather than assisting you, this mode adds resistance. It’s like walking through water and somewhat resembles a band workout. Since resistance training is my main activity, I’ve found myself grabbing the Hypershell X and wearing it while walking around the house or the yard in order to add a bit more resistance to my normal movement. My only complaint is that there’s not quite enough resistance—I want this thing to really make me sweat. Unfortunately, this is the only mode that works in any meaningful way for strength-related tasks. I had hoped that the Hypershell X would have some additional mode that helps you lift more weight or something, but the more I think about it the more dangerous that sounds. I’ve had a blast trying out the Hypershell X, and I intend to keep using it where I can fit it in. It’s incredibly fun to see the look on people’s faces when you knock it into Hyper mode and watch them walk around the room like some sort of half-person-half-robot.

item.title: REVIEW: No Manga Nails Liminal Spaces Quite Like Tsutomu Nihei’s ‘Blame!’
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
After years of replaying a conversation with an editor who described Tsutomu Nihei’s Blame! with near-religious reverence as “a masterpiece in comic storytelling,” I finally sat down to see what all the fuss was about. Having read it for myself after only experiencing Polygon Pictures’ CG film adaptation, I’m still a ways from claiming to have fully untangled every thread of its circuitous story. What I can say is that I now understand why that editor spoke about the series with such reverence, even though the reasons I fell in love with it weren’t the ones I expected. Before giving Blame! an honest try, all I could recall from the aforementioned Netflix film was a dude wandering aimlessly through a desolate sci-fi wasteland. If anything stuck with me, it was his absurdly cool gun. Even without reading the manga, the Gravitational Beam Emitter’s reputation preceded it. Its name hangs in the rafters alongside the most iconic weapons in sci-fi and manga. Basically, any problem its aptly named protagonist, Killy, encounters is immediately solved by pulling its trigger and watching a beam tear through anything fool enough to obstruct his path. Like a fool, I assumed the mystery behind his titular weapon—where it came from, how it worked, and why neither Killy nor many of his sophisticated H.R. Giger-inspired adversaries fully understood it—would be the series’ main point of intrigue. After all, Blame! itself takes its name from the thunderous onomatopoeia of the firearm before its kickback sends Killy flat on his ass or rips his arm clean off. By all accounts, the GBE seemed destined to be the thing I’d spend the entire manga obsessing over. After having finished the series, though, I couldn’t give a shit about the gun’s lore. The real star of Blame! is the liminal brutalist structures Killy roams endlessly through. Long before I felt I’d grasped Blame!‘s full scope, I found myself transfixed by the beauty and terror of its liminal spaces. On a literal level, Blame!‘s setting is a giant man-made city that Nihei suggests could be as big as our solar system. I’d go so far as to say it’s like if Backrooms folded in on itself like Demon Slayer‘s Infinity Castle. What makes Blame!‘s setting most interesting is how the endless structures Killy wanders through feel less like impossible architecture and more like an unempathetic, living organism he’s passing through. For entire stretches of chapters, Killy hardly ever comes across other people or the automatons that maintain order on its infinite floors like blood cells. All he does is traverse corridors with fleshy dead ends; he can only assume it means he’s better off not finding out why. Similarly to undarkening spots on a map in a FromSoftware game, Blame! scratches that same itch of discovery. The higher Killy climbs, the more the mystery of why this setting is so alien and fucked up unfurls. Unfortunately, whatever morsels of information Killy gleans along the way only reveal how much better off he is not knowing and getting the fuck out of dodge as soon as possible. It’s almost serene flipping through panels and picturesque double spreads that turn Killy into a Where’s Waldo speck in the vastness of Blame!‘s hulking architecture. But every once in a while that deafening silence is broken up by the sound of rubble falling. I, like Killy, know he hasn’t run into a human being for what amounts to months of his wandering. And before either his or my fight-or-flight can kick in, some wicked biomechanical apparition bursts through the floors like the Kool-Aid man, or swarms in on him like a horde of locusts. Sure, Killy inevitably shoots them away in an exciting action sequence worthy of a Mick Gordon score. But what really had me falling in love with the series was the fascination with the colossal architecture and the bizarre entities that call it home. No moment illustrates how terrifying Blame!‘s megastructure setting is more than when it introduces my favorite fear: time dilation. At one point in the manga, Killy gets separated from an ally. To me, he simply fell down a couple levels and needed to climb his way back up to meet her again. When he does, he gets hit with the wallop that, from her perspective, he’d been gone for 30 years. To my abject horror, Blame! really digs time dilation. It gets to the point where elevator rides take up to 800 hours to reach their destination. A fact that only further accentuates the manga’s other tract about what the self is when characters are able to have their consciousnesses reuploaded after their bodies are blown to shit—sometimes taking over each other’s vessels by force—but have their memories wiped. The only peer to Blame!‘s environmental storytelling is Nihei’s other series, Tower Dungeon. While I love the thematic quandary of what is the self, that pales in comparison to the sensation that every environment Killy enters existed for a millennium before his undying ass arrived and would continue stretching into infinity after he left. Not out of hostility or hospitality, but out of indifference. Blame! is bespoke architecture at its most anglerfish. That’s ultimately why I’d call Blame! a masterpiece too. item.title: REVIEW: Anker Soundcore Space 2 Pro review: Big bang for fewer bucks
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Anker Soundcore Space 2 Pro review: Big bang for fewer bucks The company’s latest headphones rival Apple, Bose and Sony at a much lower price. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. If you don't like the idea of paying $350 to $500 for a set of flagship headphones, Anker's Soundcore line offers a lot of performance at much lower prices. Over the years, the company has refined its formula by balancing sound and features in various packages so as to compete with the likes of Apple, Bose, Sony and Sennheiser. With the Space 2 Pro, Anker put its new Thus audio chip in headphones for the first time, making lofty claims about the upgraded voice clarity as a result. At $200, these aren't just an affordable alternative to the big names in headphones, they're a worthy contender in their own right. What's good about the Space 2 Pro? The first thing that stood out to me about the Space 2 Pro is the design. These do not look like they cost $200, especially not the grey version that I tested. Anker refined the look of the Space line here for a premium aesthetic and a build that's lightweight, but not overly plastic. The sliders for fit adjustments are metal and both the headband and ear pads are wrapped in soft leather. There are also subtle metallic accents to complete the premium design, like the circles on the outside of the ear cups and subtly placed product name. Even though the Space 2 Pro is the flagship Soundcore headphones, the price tag pits them up against decidedly midrange competition. Design-wise, the Space 2 Pro is vastly superior in that category, and that advantage continues into audio performance. These headphones have more bass and overall clarity than you'll typically find in the $200 range. The 35mm drivers are made with two different materials in order to maximize both high-end clarity and deep bass. When I listened to Mastodon's Marrow Deep, Brann Dailor's drums boom throughout and Troy Sanders' bass provides the backbone for the guitar riffs. Thanks to Anker's "crystalline highs" here, guitars and synths cut through the mix clearly, so you never miss a note of Bill Kelliher's handiwork. The overall clarity and detail on the Space 2 Pro is really on display with more acoustic-driven genres, like Zach Bryan's Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs. The piano, acoustic guitar and string section seem to float behind the interwoven vocals of Bryan and Lana Del Rey on "Lies," for example. Anker is very proud that the Space 2 Pro currently holds the Guiness World Record for the "clearest over-ear headphones for calls." I was immediately skeptical that this would hold any weight in real-world use, but boy was I wrong. Plenty of headphones manage to nullify background noise, but they do so at great expense to voice clarity. But thanks to that Thus chip and a six-microphone array, the Space 2 Pro offers extremely clear voice performance while effectively blocking background noise. Not only do they combat would-be distractions exceptionally well, they do so without making you sound even the slightest bit robotic. I thought I sounded pretty close to how I did in a quiet room when the processing kicked in, maybe only the slightest bit muffled, but never like a digitized version of myself. The company promises battery life of up to 30 hours when you have active noise cancellation (ANC) on, or up to 60 hours with it off. During my testing, which I conducted almost entirely with noise cancellation enabled, I got 31 hours before the Space 2 Pro shut off. I did take a call or two a day where I needed to switch to transparency mode so I didn't feel the need to shout to hear myself speaking, but I'd say 95 percent of the time, I was using ANC. What's not so great about the Space 2 Pro? The most disappointing aspect of the Space 2 Pro to me are a number of subpar audio features. The Thus chip powers what Anker calls Hear ID 5.0, a feature that uses a hearing test to customize the sound of the headphones to your preferences. I didn't think the resulting tailored audio profile offered any meaningful improvement over the stock tuning, neither did spatial audio settings or the collection of curated presets. I tested all of them, of course, but every time I used one, I found myself longing for the out-of-the-box sound after just a few minutes of use. Anker boasts Adaptive ANC 3.0 on the Space 2 Pro, a noise-canceling setup that relies on the Thus chip and eight microphones to combat background noise. The company specifically lists "blocking office chatter and keyboard clicks for instant silence" among the headphones' strengths. While I do think the Space 2 Pro does an above average job of lowering the volume on human voices, and it definitely blocks keyboard clicks, its general noise canceling abilities are just okay. The headphones struggled with constant noise sources, like white noise machines and particularly raucous fans. On Anker's flagship earbuds, the Liberty 5 Pro Max, the company built an AI note taking assistant into the charging case (which has a touchscreen). Even though the Space 2 Pro doesn't have a case, it does have plenty of microphones, and "AI Note-Taker" is currently listed as "TBD" on the spec sheet. If that feature does eventually arrive, there are two potential issues with it. First, it will be a lot more awkward to wear over-ear headphones in a meeting than it would be to slide a small earbuds case to the middle of the table. Second, if you plan to regularly use Anker's transcription service and cloud storage, you'll have to pay for a subscription. You only get two hours of transcriptions and 10,000 minutes of audio storage monthly for free, and only for two years. Plans are then either $8.33 or $20 per month (billed annually) depending on your needs. Since it's unclear if this feature will ever arrive, its absence doesn't impact my overall assessment. It's easy to dismiss Soundcore as merely a budget brand, but that would be a mistake. With products like the Space 2 Pro, Anker proves it can hang with the best, offering comparable performance for significantly less money. In fact, I'd argue if voice clarity is your primary factor in choosing a new set of headphones, this model should be your first choice. For many, though, that's further down the list of priorities. While there are caveats when it comes to ANC performance, audio features and a (potentially) unnecessary note taker, the Space 2 Pro has a lot of premium traits. The overall sound quality is good, the design is refined, the fit is comfortable and battery life claims hold true. At a time when the best overall headphones you can buy are $460 at full price, Anker's ability to produce a $200 alternative that won't disappoint you is no small feat.

item.title: SALES: Re-releases of Wing Commander, Ultima titles hit Steam and GOG
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica
Many people are not big fans of game publisher EA right now for good reason, but for those who remember a better time in the 1990s, there’s a little good news. Twenty-five classic games from that EA era have been lightly remastered and updated, then placed for sale on Steam and GOG, including several Wing Commander games and nearly the entire Ultima series. Below is the full list of remastered or re-released games: - Wing Commander: 35th Anniversary Edition - Wing Commander II: Vengeance of the Kilrathi: 35th Anniversary Edition - Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger: 30th Anniversary Edition - Wing Commander IV: The Price of Freedom: 30th Anniversary Edition - Wing Commander Prophecy: 30th Anniversary Edition - Privateer 2: The Darkening: 30th Anniversary Edition - Ultima II: The Revenge of the Enchantress In a lengthy blog post published this week, Jim Vessella, a senior producer at EA, described the efforts that went into remastering Wing Commander I-IV and Prophecy, Privateer 2, and Road Rash. It’s a long, detailed story that’s worth reading yourself, but here’s a top-level summary. After working on the mostly widely acclaimed Command & Conquer: Remastered Collection in 2019, Vessella writes that he learned about and visited a room at EA’s Redwood Shores campus that contained a large archive of poorly labeled or sorted physical media from ages past. In his free time, and with the help of others, he began cataloging this archive and discovered, among other things, that it contained virtually the entirety of the original masters of Wing Commander III and Wing Commander IV‘s full-motion-video cutscenes. The story that ensues involves building a small team of contractors, poring through the footage 17 hours a day on swing shifts to label and digitize it, and then coordinating with several key community members—particularly Matt Wells, who has made community enhancement patches for some of the Wing Commander games—to put together remasters of those games.
