item.title: SALES: Can't Afford Brand New Tech This Holiday Season? Shop Refurbished and Save Some Money
item.description:
Source: PCMag
The ongoing memory shortage has raised the cost of laptops, desktops, phones, and other tech. Even gaming consoles like the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and Nintendo Switch 2 have seen price jumps this year. With the holidays approaching, does that mean you'll have to pay hundreds more for tech gifts? Not if you shop refurbished instead. There's a clear reason to buy a refurb instead of a brand-new device: it's cheaper. Like-new items aren't subject to tariff-induced inflation (since they're already in the US) or a parts shortage (since they're already built). Plus, it's nice to avoid sending another gadget to the landfill. In a 2026 research study conducted by PCMag parent company Ziff Davis, over three-quarters of the respondents said they'd prefer to upgrade their device only when the new ones are clearly worth the hassle and price. The problem is that refurbished products had a life before you. Maybe it was a short existence with a careful original owner, but maybe not. Here's a quick rundown of what you should know before you click the buy button on a renewed or revamped piece of hardware. If you can't get these questions answered to your satisfaction, stick with purchasing brand-new products, if possible (and affordable). 1. Is It a Refurb or Open-Box Return? A typical open-box product was purchased, opened, and returned before use. Maybe the buyer or recipient decided they didn't want it, or perhaps the packaging was damaged, so it was sent back unused as a precaution. I'd argue that to be a true refurb, a device should require some kind of repair, cleaning, or sprucing up. Legally, though, there's no actual definition of "refurbished.” It can signify whatever a vendor or seller wants it to mean. You may also see terms like "pre-owned" and "reconditioned," which are synonyms—until they're not. All returned, resold products tend to be lumped together, regardless of condition. Thankfully, US laws prevent companies from selling returned products as if they were brand-new. That's beneficial to you, since the price should drop once a product has the refurbished label. Ask the seller about a product’s origin and hope for an open-box product; you may not be the first owner, but you could be the first user. 2. Who Did the Refurbishing? Not all restorations are alike. It's possible that a third party did the work and is reselling the product. Sticking with the original company handling the work is the smarter move. It will have the right packaging and parts to make the product as close to new as possible. Look for "factory-certified" or similar nomenclature. That said, you can see real savings from a third-party refurbishment. However, some describe this arena as the Wild West, as there's no way to determine a product's quality until you've already bought it. Buyer beware! 3. Does It Come With All the Stuff? Refurbished products often lack the accessories included with a new purchase. That's another reason to try to find manufacturer-refurbished units; you're more likely to get all the parts. You might also get the product in packaging similar to the original, if that's important to you. 4. Does the Product Still Have a Warranty? Don't buy any product marked "as-is," because that removes any implied warranty the product might carry. The buyer risks getting hardware that may not even work properly. Just because a device can turn on doesn't mean it can go online, get a signal, etc. By law, used products in many states are covered by an implied warranty. A device has to be able to do what it was designed to do, even if sold used. A phone has to make calls (phones still do that, I'm told). A laptop must boot up and connect to the internet. A webcam had better make you look good in that Zoom meeting. Your best bet is to ask the seller whether a warranty or guarantee exists. It's more likely if the original manufacturer refurbished the device. Without a warranty, the price discount may not be worth the risk. Also, confirm the warranty length. Six months for a device that originally had one year's protection is risky. There are no rules for grading a refurbished product, except that the seller can't claim it's brand-new. They can, however, say it's "like new." That might mean the item was never used. It could also mean that the product was refurbished after a hard life. Maybe a scratched or cracked screen was replaced. If you can find out, it's worth knowing exactly what "like new" means. After "like new," the options are all "used" in some form, from "gently" on down. You'll find variations on that language from site to site and vendor to vendor. 6. What's the Return Policy? It takes a while to notice problems in some products. You want at least a month-long return window (that's not much to ask, given that companies selling giant mattresses give you 100 days). That should go for refurbished products as well. If you can't get at least two weeks to futz with a product that offers a no-cost return option, don't bother. Many sellers will say "sale final," and you don't want that (unless the savings are truly astronomical). Always read the fine print. And the moment you open a refurbed product, thoroughly inspect it. You might want to take advantage of that return policy right away. 7. What Should I Not Buy Refurbished? We recommend avoiding the following refurbished products: - Items that touch your skin a lot, such as headphones and earbuds - Hard drives or solid-state drives, as they can't really be reset to factory settings - TVs, as it's hard to tell how used a TV might be Some of those purchases might be OK if you trust the company behind the product's renewal. Conversely, you should only buy refurbished products from select companies because their new products are too expensive (cough, Apple, cough).

item.title: SALES: Want to Play Switch Games on Switch 2? Here's How Much It'll Cost You
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Video game prices have been slowly creeping up for years. When the Nintendo Switch first launched in 2017, full-priced games were $60. Then, PlayStation and Xbox first-party releases jumped to $70 in 2020. Nintendo followed suit in 2023 with The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom. But Switch 2 pricing has made everything more complicated. Mario Kart World costs $80. Donkey Kong Bananza is $70. Yet Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade is just $40. Want to buy physical games? That will cost you more than the digital versions. And even though some of the Switch 1 games I own are backward compatible, if I want to upgrade to the Switch 2 version for better performance or additional DLC, the upgrade pricing is all over the place. In some cases, upgrading costs $0, while others require you to break out your credit card. Grand Theft Auto 6 may cost you as much as $100 at launch, and it feels only a matter of time before Nintendo does the same. Here's the full breakdown of how much it costs to upgrade your old Switch game to the Switch 2 version. Before I talk about how much the upgrades cost, I need to explain the three (yes, three) different kinds of games you can play on the Switch 2. - Switch 2 games: These are native Switch 2 games made exclusively for the console. They feature the Switch 2 logo and are designed to take advantage of the latest hardware. This includes Mario Kart World and Donkey Kong Bananza, as well as third-party releases like Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition. - Switch 2 Edition games: These are Switch games that have performance and visual upgrades over their Switch 1 counterparts. The physical versions of these titles will have the Switch game and Upgrade Pack on the same cartridge. Metroid Prime 4: Beyond and Pokémon Legends: Z-A are Switch 2 Edition games, and are labeled accordingly. - Switch 1 games: Finally, there are just Switch 1 games, since (most of) these can be played on the Switch 2. This means you can play Breath of the Wild or Metroid Dread for free if you already own those games. They won't have the significant upgrades that come with the Upgrade Packs, but should gain some small benefits simply by running on more powerful hardware. How Much Does Nintendo Charge for a Switch 2 Upgrade Pack? Instead of having to buy new titles to get upgraded versions of the titles you already own, Nintendo allows you to upgrade your Switch games into native Switch 2 games, turning them into Switch 2 Edition games. However, the cost of that upgrade varies widely, depending on how much new content is included. Right now, Nintendo sells its so-called Upgrade Packs at four separate price points: - $20: Upgrade Packs that include DLC-sized additions for the Switch 2 cost $20. This includes Super Mario Party Jamboree, Kirby and the Forgotten Land, and Super Mario Bros. Wonder, which add new gameplay features and content to the base game. The Switch 2 Edition versions of these games cost $80, so it's the $60 base game + $20 DLC. - $10: Games with smaller performance and visual upgrades, such as Metroid Prime 4: Beyond and Pokémon Legends: Z-A, cost $10. Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom are also priced here because a new copy of BOTW for Switch 2 costs $70 and TOTK costs $80. However, they're actually included as part of Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack. It's interesting to note that the Xenoblade games add some additional content. - $5: Nintendo introduced a $5 upgrade path for the Switch 2 Edition of Animal Crossing: New Horizons to coincide with the game's free version 3.0 update. This upgrade adds enhanced visuals, GameChat functionality, and mouse controls. Xenoblade Chronicles X is another $5 upgrade, but it just includes performance improvements. Interestingly, both games are getting new physical editions, so is this the one common thread? - Free: Finally, some games have received free updates from Nintendo, including Arms, Pokémon Scarlet/Violet, The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom, Super Mario Odyssey, Bowser's Fury, and more. These updates mainly focus on visual upgrades, though some gain frame rate bumps, HDR, and even GameChat support. - Clubhouse Games: 51 Worldwide Classics How Much Are Third-Party Games? It's not just Nintendo games that have unlockable updates for the Switch 2; all developers have the option of offering an upgrade path to players. Many of these updates come with graphic and performance improvements, but some may add additional content. However, how much this costs will depend on the game and the publisher. For instance, games in Hamster's Arcade Archives line cost $2.99 to upgrade. Meanwhile, Marvelous has multiple games at the $10 price point. However, many developers have opted not to charge for the Switch 2 Edition of their game. This means if you own the Switch version, the upgrade is available to you as a free download.

item.title: SALES: Best monitor arms 2026: Expert picks for single- and dual-monitors setups
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
A monitor arm is a sure way to boost the effectiveness of a home office setup. A good-quality arm not only frees up usable space on your desk’s surface, it aids ergonomics by allowing you to move and position your display/s for optimal comfort. Plus, a monitor arm makes your office setup look really pro. The only catch is the price. Most monitor arms worth buying will cost close to $200, and heavy-duty arms capable of holding two large displays can be priced even higher. The good news is that a good-quality monitor arm is likely to last you for a very long time. That’s why it’s important to make the right choice when you purchase a monitor arm. To help you with that, we’ve tested several popular monitor arms, for both single- and dual-monitor setups. Below you’ll find our curated list of recommendations, with detailed explanations of what features and qualities make them stand out. We even have some good budget recommendations. Below our picks, we point out some arms that we aren’t so keen on — to provide a point of comparison. Why you should trust PCWorld for monitor arm reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name! PCWorld has been covering PCs since 1983. That includes PC hardware of all types, including monitors and monitor accessories. All of our recommendations have been tested hands-on and vetted by our expert reviewers, who’ve applied not only performance benchmarks but rigorous usability standards. Ergotron LX Pro – Best single-monitor arm The Ergotron LX Pro is a practical, effective, easy-to-use monitor arm. Ergotron achieves this ease-of-install with clever, yet simple, engineering. The LX Pro’s clamp mechanism, which secures the monitor to a desk, takes the extra step of providing a comfortable handhold that makes it easy to work the clamp without tools. The arm’s two sections, meanwhile, simply slip into place. Ergotron also provides thumb screws for attaching the arm’s VESA mount to the back of your monitor. Depending on your monitor, you may need to use the included hex wrench to tighten the components. Otherwise, installation doesn’t require tools. The arm’s desk clamp mechanism is wide, which is important. Clamps with a small surface concentrate more force on your desk and cause damage if over-tightened. A wider clamp better distributes the force. That means the LX Pro is less likely to damage weaker desks (though caution when tightening the clamp is recommended). Fortunately, the arm’s ease of installation doesn’t lead to functional downsides. The arm can support monitors up to 34 inches diagonally that weigh up to 22 pounds. The arm also lifts up to 13 inches, tilts up to 85 degrees, and can swivel and rotate to a full 360 degrees. Cables are routed through channels in the arm and secured by sturdy detachable cladding. Ergotron provides a 10-year warranty. The LX Pro even fixes our gripes about its predecessor, the Ergotron LX. The LX Pro’s base is more compact, the white colorway now has a color-coordinated VESA mount, and the new design is more attractive. The only downgrade compared to the old Ergotron LX is a lower maximum weight (the LX could handle up to 25 pounds). But that’s unlikely to matter, as 32-inch and 34-inch monitors usually weigh 15 pounds or less. The LX Pro’s $209 MSRP is enough to make shoppers think twice, but it’s great value for money. The arm’s overall build quality feels competitive with more expensive monitor arms, such as the Humanscale M2.1. That makes the Ergotron LX Pro an easy recommendation. It’s simple to set up, looks nice, works well in day-to-day use, yet remains affordable. We already liked the Ergotron LX, but the LX Pro is a great upgrade. MSI MAG MT201 – Best budget single-monitor arm The MSI MAG MT201 is an inexpensive monitor arm that’s rated to support 49-inch screens that weight up to 44 pounds. That’s high enough that it’s unnecessary; even my 42-inch LG B4 television weighs only 25 pounds. The MAG MT201 has a spring (rather than gas or gas-spring hybrid) tension system that proved capable of handling the 32-inch monitors I had on hand. Setting up the MAG MT201 is a bit complicated. The stand’s assembly requires multiple steps and tightening numerous screws. Tools are provided, but it will take about 15 to 20 minutes to finish. This is something that separates the MAG MT201R from more expensive arms, like the top-rated Ergotron LX Pro. The steps required to assemble each monitor arm are similar, but the MT201 requires more screws, and some screws in awkward positions. Adjusting the monitor is less difficult. The arm itself felt sturdy and swivels left and right, as well as up and down, without trouble. You’ll want an Allen-head screwdriver handy, though, as several adjustments including the monitor arm neck and height tension require it. The arm includes a quick-release VESA mount, meaning you can detach a monitor from it by removing a single thumb-screw. It’s a nice feature to have on a budget arm. Aside from a prominent MSI logo, the monitor arm looks sleek, professional, and reserved, and could work equally well for a home office or a gaming setup. Build quality isn’t amazing, with plastic cladding over metal framing, but it’s a looker for a budget monitor arm. It’s better than the industrial look of the Monoprice monitor arm (our former budget pick) and more distinctive than budget arms from Huanuo and Vivo. The MAG MT201 also delivers a massive gain in quality over arms in the $25 to $50 bracket, most of which are less adjustable and even more difficult to set up. Price works in the MSI MAG MT201’s favor. It carries an MSRP of $99.99, but it’s often on Amazon for around $60 to $80, with an all-time low price of $49.99. That makes the MSI MAG MT201 feel like the minimum viable monitor arm. Buying anything less expensive doesn’t make sense, as you’ll sacrifice too much in quality and design. Huanuo HNSS6 Single Monitor Arm – Best single-monitor arm under $50 The Huanuo HNSS6 Single Monitor Arm is easily our go-to recommendation for shoppers looking to buy the least expensive monitor arm that can still fulfill its job. The arm comes in two pieces: The lower portion swivels while the upper portion allows for height, tilt, and rotation adjustments. A gas spring provides tension to keep monitors aloft, which is an upgrade from the clips and screws used by the least expensive arms. However, it’s worth noting that gas springs can lose their potency over time. These features are typical for the price: Most competitors are similar in design and use a gas cylinder. What makes the Huanuo a winner is its overall quality and ease of install. Setup required installation of just three screws (and adjustment to a couple more). The clamp used to mount the arm to the desk was intuitive compared to rivals like the MountUp Single Monitor Arm, as the spacing of the clamp is adjustable without removing and re-installing screws to secure it. The arm claims to hold 32-inch displays up to 20 pounds, which is enough to hold most monitors. We tested it with panels up to 32 inches weighing up to 12 pounds, and it supported those with ease. One notable downside is cable management. The plastic covers provided are finicky and won’t hold many wires, so if you want to add USB cables in addition to a video connection and power, you’re probably out of luck. To be fair, though, the same is true of most inexpensive arms. The Huanuo wasn’t as easy to set up or adjust as the Ergotron LX, our favorite overall pick, and it’s not as sturdy as the Monoprice Single Monitor Arm, which typically sells for $60. Still, the Huanuo gets the job done. Herman Miller Flo – Best premium single-monitor arm Want a monitor arm that gets the job done and looks good doing it? The Herman Miller Flo is for you. The Flo’s design sets it apart from the pack. Herman Miller ditches the angular, industrial design of many competitors for a smooth, natural look. While clearly designed for a corporate office, it also fits in with a home office setup, where its friendly, approachable look helps it blend in with its surroundings. The Flo is backed by a 12-year warranty and offers 24/7 customer service, so that extra spend is also buying you peace of mind. It’s easy to set up and use. The monitor’s clamp works similarly to other monitor arms I tested, but it’s more refined and requires fewer screws (a grommet is also available). The VESA mount is also excellent, providing a simple clip design that’s secure and can be easily pre-mounted to a monitor for simple installation. The way this mount works accommodates monitors that have a slightly recessed mount position, which may cause problems for other monitor arms. The monitor’s range of adjustment isn’t much different from other high-end monitor arms. It offers 13.3 inches of vertical adjustment, 80 degrees of tilt, and 360 degrees of swivel and rotation. That’s essentially identical to the less expensive Ergotron LX. The Flo’s operation is smoother, however: I found I could adjust a monitor’s height with a mere nudge, making this a good choice if you tend to adjust your monitor’s position regularly. Surprisingly, the Flo has a listed weight limit of 20 pounds and recommends use with monitors weighing at least 7 pounds. Most monitors fit within this range, but some heavier models won’t be compatible with the Flo. Herman Miller lists the Flo at $295, which is a lot to ask for a single-monitor arm. The Ergotron LX offers similar features at a much lower price. However, the Flo is a smoother, more appealing monitor arm, and worth the upgrade if you want form with your function. Ergotron HX – Best heavy-duty single-monitor arm It’s natural, given the only slight difference in name, to think the Ergotron HX is merely an uprated version of the Ergotron LX. That’s not the case. This is an entirely different monitor arm which pairs its increased capacity with improved build quality and a more professional look. This is a good choice for anyone who uses heavier displays. First, let’s talk weight. The Ergotron HX is rated to hold monitors that weigh up to 42 pounds and screen sizes up to 49 inches. That’s an extraordinarily high weight limit—I haven’t reviewed a single monitor in 2023 that exceeds it. I attached both a 32-inch widescreen and 38-inch ultrawide monitor, which weighed roughly 15 and 20 pounds, respectively, and the HX easily handled both. The use of plastic is minimal and reserved for small portions of cladding that appear used only for cable routing. The arm’s moving parts include larger, sturdier mechanisms, and felt extremely smooth in my use. Ergotron backs the arm with a 10-year warranty. The monitors range of adjustment is a bit limited compared to the LX. It offers 11.5 inches of height, 75 degrees of tilt, 180 degrees of swivel, and 360 degrees of rotation. However, a somewhat more limited height adjustment is typical in this category due to the size of monitors these stands are expected to carry. The monitor arm’s impressive design also provides a more robust look. This could be a con for some, however, as the arm can seem a bit…much in a home office setup. It’s an expensive arm, as well. Expect to pay about $350. The Ergotron HX is an obvious choice if you want to mount an ultrawide, super-ultrawide, or large format widescreen monitor on your desk. Humanscale M2.1 with M/Connect – Best monitor arm w/ built-in dock The Humanscale M2.1 with M/Connect laptop docking station is an attractive, robust, and modern monitor arm that can expand your laptop’s connectivity without taking up additional space on your desktop. Humanscale’s entry-level M2.1 doesn’t include a laptop dock, but it’s designed to accommodate the M/Connect 3, which nestles snuggly into the base of the arm. Most home office shoppers will likely choose the M/Connect 3 USB Data Hub, which currently retails for $253 (on top of the M2.1’s base price of $356). The hub adds three USB-C ports and two USB-A ports. If you want even more ports, the $600 M/Connect 3 Pro Dock adds two more USB-A ports, two more USB-C, Ethernet, and two DisplayPort ports. The M/Connect 3’s added connectivity is an excellent way to expand the ports on a laptop. Its central location makes the ports easy to access and keeps them firmly located in a set position on your desk (as opposed to freestanding hubs and adapters, which tend to get shoved around, or off, a desk). It’s also a good alternative to a USB-C monitor. We like USB-C monitors, but packing connectivity into the monitor can make it difficult to access some ports, as most are located on the rear of the display. Connectivity aside, the Humanscale M2.1 is a robust, if conventional, monitor arm. It can handle monitors between 5 and 15 pounds, which is enough to support the vast majority of widescreen monitors under 32 inches in size. It also has a “smart stop” feature, which lets users customize the amount of rotation the arm allows, and easy-to-use quick release joints that are handy when disassembling or moving the arm. The arm isn’t as smooth in operation as the Herman Miller Flo, but it remains easy enough to adjust. While the above picks are focused on single-monitor arms, we know that many people (this author included) are incapable of functioning effectively without a two-monitor setup. Fortunately, there are a number of worthy monitor arms that support dual monitors off a single mount. When shopping for a dual-monitor arm, pay attention to the combined supported weight and make sure your monitors won’t exceed it. Also note the range of monitor alignment that’s allowed. And finally, understand the desk footprint that’s involved with a particular dual-monitor mount, as well as the complexity of the setup. Below are the best dual-monitor arms that we recommend. Ergotron LX Dual Monitor Arm – Best dual-monitor arm Two monitors are always better than one, and the same goes for monitor arms. It’s no surprise, then, that Ergotron’s LX Side-by-Side ranks as our best dual monitor arm. The Ergotron LX Side-by-Side pairs two LX monitor arms together on one mount. The look, feel, and specifications of each arm are close to its standalone sibling. Monitor size is one exception: While the standard LX is rated for monitors up to 34 inches, the Side-by-Side’s arm is only rated for monitors up to 27 inches. The monitor arms aren’t long enough to fit two 32-inch or 34-inch monitors side-by-side. Vertical arrangements are also supported, though only if one of the two monitors is small (less than 23 inches diagonal). Look and feel is otherwise similar to the standard Ergotron LX, and that’s why the dual monitor arm also earns a recommendation. The dual-monitor arm provides the same winning balance of build quality, adjustability, and smooth operation, and it’s backed by the same 10-year warranty. Pricing is a bit higher at $470, which is a slight savings compared to buying two LX arms individually. Workstream by Monoprice Dual Monitor Arm – Best budget dual-monitor arm The same logic that applies to our favorite dual monitor arm also to the budget model, giving Monoprice’s Workstream Dual Monitor Arm a clear path to victory. In fact, the dual arm’s pricing is even more impressive. The Workstream Dual Monitor is four times less expensive than the Ergotron LX Side-by-Side. I’m a bit shocked by the quality Monoprice can offer at a $100 price point. Ergotron’s alternative is more attractive and easier to use, but is it four times better? That’s a tough call. The Workstream’s downsides are identical to standard model. Build quality is impressive for the price, but the arm is difficult to set up and not as smooth in operation. I’m also doubtful the arm is capable of handling two 20-pound monitors, as its spec sheets claim. Fortunately, 27-inch monitors (the largest this arm can handle side-by-side) usually weigh less than 10 pounds, so weight capacity shouldn’t be an issue. Clearspace Uni-2 – Best premium dual-monitor arm The Clearspace Uni-2’s design is a bit different from most competitors. It places two individual arms on a single pole. Each arm can adjust for height, swivel, and tilt, and each monitor mounts to an “independent slider” which can move right or left, making it easier to tune the placement of each monitor relative to the other. Compared to the Humanscale M8.1, I found the Uni-2 easier to adjust. However, the Humanscale M8.1’s beefy crossbar is likely to prove more stable if you’re mounting large monitors. Besides offering a high degree of adjustability, the Clearspace Uni-2 looks great, and that’s important. Competitors from Humanscale and Herman Miller also look luxurious but have a more corporate or “executive’s office” vibe. The Uni-2’s softer look feels more appropriate for a home office. Clearspace also provides black, silver, and white colorways, and every component of each colorway is molded in the promised color (which isn’t true of most competitors). Clearspace also throws in subtle touches, like soft-touch inserts on the side of each monitor arm. That’s the kind of design a home office user will appreciate. Clearspace also looks to separate itself with connectivity. The Uni-2 comes standard Smart Hub that provides a single USB-A and USB-C port. That’s a small edge over competitors, which often sell the dock as an upgrade. Owners can improve the basic hub with the optional SmartDock (pictured), which expands connectivity to include additional USB ports, HDMI, and Ethernet. Unfortunately, I can’t recommend it: The SmartDock is priced at $650 yet lacks support for features I’d expect at that price, like 4K 60Hz video and 2.5Gbps Ethernet. While the optional SmartDock is a miss, the arm is a winner. The Clearspace Uni-2 is expensive, but the price can be justified if you’re picky about the look and feel of your home office space. Clearspace also offers a single-monitor and triple-monitor arm: While I didn’t test them, I expect they’d offer similar perks. The MSI MPG MT201R is a heavy-duty monitor arm that’s rated to support 49-inch screens that weigh up to 44 pounds. It supports that weight with a gas spring mount. While that might sound like a lot, you shouldn’t think it makes the arm any more durable than another. Most monitors, even large ones, weigh less than 25 pounds, anyway. Unboxing and setting up the MPG MT201R can take a while, as the stand comes in numerous parts connected by numerous screws. The tools are provided, and the included assembly guide is clear enough, but more expensive monitor arms usually ship with fewer parts. The monitor includes a VESA quick release feature that makes it easy to attach or detach a monitor by removing a single thumb screw. The C-Clamp plate is broad and the base of the stand is also large. Together, these make for a very secure fit that is less likely to damage a desk, because the load of the clamp’s force is spread out more evenly. MSI’s branding is prominent, and I don’t think that’s a plus. The monitor arm will only look “right” with an MSI MPG monitor. Even then, I don’t think MSI’s design across its product line is coherent enough to justify buying an MSI arm to go with an MSI monitor. On the plus side, the arm has RGB lighting which runs through the arm itself. The lighting is powered by USB-A. It doesn’t sync with other devices, but it looks nice. Pricing is a bit awkward. The MSI MPG MT201R has an MSRP of $129.99 and often sells at that price, though it’s occasionally reduced to $99.99. That’s fair, but aside from the RGB lighting, I don’t think the MPG MT201R adds much value over a less expensive arm like the MSI MAG MT201 or the Workstream by Monoprice monitor arm. I’m also not sold on the design, which seems meant to appeal only to MSI super-fans. Huanuo TitanLift (HNSS48) The Huanuo TitanLift’s name implies it’s a heavy-duty monitor arm, and it delivers. Huanuo doubles down on “heavy duty” with thick components mostly made of metal and has a big, secure base. If you like your trucks with lots of diamond-cut plating, or you think flannel shirts are the last word in functional fashion, this arm is for you. But it’s not all just for show. The arm claims to hold up to 40 pounds, which is a lot—the heaviest display I have weighs in at about 30 pounds and it’s a TV. You’ll be hard pressed to find a monitor, even a 49-inch super-ultrawide, that comes close to the arm’s weight limit. There’s also a wide range of ergonomic adjustment. In addition to height adjustment the arm provides 50 degrees of tilt, 90 degrees of swivel, and 360 degrees of rotation. Adjustment is a bit stiff out of the box but can be loosened with an included Allen wrench. We generally like the Huanuo TitanLift and can recommend it when the arm is on sale for about $20 less than its competitors, such as the MSI MAG MT201, though a few minor points prevent it from earning a broader recommendation. Setting up the monitor arm is a chore. You’ll need to install multiple screws and the base uses two clamps, each of which must be screwed to the base individually. The tilt mechanism is a bit odd, too. When tilting up it feels a bit loose until it clicks into place, after which the mechanism feels tight. It works, but it’s not as smooth as it could be. These shortcomings are minor, though, and we enjoyed our time with the arm. The MSI MAG MT201 is slightly easier to set up and looks a bit nicer, but the Huanuo TitanLift is a reasonable alternative. Both arms are a good pick at their sub-$100 price points. The MSI MPG MT161R is an affordable single monitor arm built for gamers who want something with some flair. It has a spring mechanism that can support screens up to 45 inches that weigh up to about 35 pounds. Design is what sets the MPG MT161R apart. It uses plastic cladding to create a dramatic, mechanical look with sharp edges and a bit of red trim. The centerpiece, however, is undoubtedly the monitor arm’s base. It uses RGB lighting and reflective material to create a fun hall-of-mirrors effect. The lighting is powered by USB-A. The extensive use of plastic cladding over the arm’s metal components is not to the arm’s credit, however. It feels spindly and inexpensive. To be fair, it’s an affordable arm with an MSRP of $109.99—but I think a price around $75 would be more in line with the quality of the arm. While the RGB lighting is fun, it’s limited to the base of the arm and doesn’t sync with other devices. Setting up the arm is a bit finicky. The arm ships in numerous pieces and requires installation of numerous screws. Tools are included, and the assembly manual is adequate, but it’s annoying. The monitor includes a quick-release VESA mount which allows a monitor to be removed or reattached using a thumbscrew. While I appreciate MSI’s attempt to design an arm that looks different, it’s hard to recommend the result. Many less expensive arms are at least as functional and the design, though unique, doesn’t seem worth much of a premium. I can only recommend it if you fancy the arm’s look. The MountUp MU0004 Single Monitor Arm seems like an even more affordable alternative to the Huanuo HNSS6. They look similar in photos, and each has a gas spring. However, the MountUp’s lower price — usually $5 to $10 less than the Huanuo — comes with some compromises. The MountUp arm was more difficult to install. This is due to the clamp, which has a two-piece design that requires screws be removed and re-installed when adjusting the clamp’s size. Adjustment of the clamp was also a bit more difficult, as turning the knob required more force, and the clamp lacks a rubberized pad to prevent it from marking the underside of your desk. We also didn’t like the MountUp’s fit and finish. It had a coarse, matte feel that seemed more industrial than the Huanuo, and miles behind the Ergotron LX. It’s not all bad news. MonutUp says the monitor arm can support 32-inch displays up to 17 pounds. That’s rather heavy for a modern monitor, and it easily handled a 32-inch display weighing 12 pounds. While inferior to the Huanuo, the MonutUp could work if you don’t mind fiddling with a few more screws during installation and can overlooks is lackluster build quality. Still, it’s hard to justifying paying $30 for the MonutUp if you can bug the Huanuo for $40 (or even $50). A monitor arm can last for years, so spending a few extra bucks for a better experience makes sense. At the time we bought it for testing, the Vivo STAND-V002 was ranked as the second best-selling monitor arm on Amazon. That’s a shame, because it’s easily the worst arm we’ve tested so far. To be fair, it’s also the least expensive. The STAND-V002 is typically sold below $30. That’s less than many top-selling single monitor arms! Vivo achieves that by cutting the arm’s features to the bone. Adjustability is minimal, so much so that Vivo (mostly) advertises the STAND-V002 as a “desk mount” or “stand” instead of an arm. It has a clamp, a pole, and two jointed arms that attach to the pole at a single point. You can adjust the monitors for height, but only together: One can’t be higher than the other. The arms, meanwhile, have joints that allow swivel and adjustment side-to-side, as well as tilt up and down. You can’t adjust these on-the-fly, though, because everything is tensioned by screws that must be loosened with a tool, adjusted, and then re-tightened to keep the monitors in place. Build quality is poor. Vivo claims the arms can hold two monitors up to 22 pounds each, but we noticed a slight deflection downward even when attaching a 27-inch display weighing 10 pounds. Cable management is provided by plastic clips that are barely adequate to the task and tend to fall off when jostled. The clamp is small and lacks a rubber pad, so it could mark softer woods and materials. We suppose the Vivo could work if you plan to mount a couple 24-inch monitors and don’t care about adjusting them once in place, but it’s otherwise not worth $30. It’s cheap, sure — but in our experience, monitor arms this cheap tend to fall apart after a couple years (or less). Humanscale is synonymous with high-end office furniture: The Freedom chair is something of an icon in executive offices across the globe. But Humanscale’s high-end office hardware is at times an awkward fit for a home office, as the M8.1 demonstrates. The Humanscale M8.1 looks similar to the M2.1, but it’s upgraded to handle monitors between 6 and 28 pounds (almost double the M2.1 in our list above). That’s enough to handle nearly any monitor available today, including large ultrawides like the Dell Ultrasharp U4025QW. The arm can also handle two monitors of the appropriate combined weight and offers a “crossbar” to support them both on a single arm. That’s good, and useful, but pricing is an obstacle. The arm starts at $545, but the crossbar (required to use two monitors) ups the price to $686. The M/Connect 3 laptop dock is also available to the M8.1 but, of course, adds even more to the price. That’s a bit hard to accept when the Ergotron HX, which supports monitors up to 42 pounds, starts at $350, or $585 for the dual-monitor crossbar version. Ergotron’s alternative feels as sturdy, supports even larger and heavier displays, and is less expensive. The Humanscale M8.1 has features you won’t find on the Ergotron, such as an optional laptop dock and customizable arm rotation, and it’s a fine selection if price is no obstacle. In most cases, though, the M8.1’s price will be hard to justify. Huanuo’s HNDS6 is a budget dual-monitor arm that’s popular on Amazon (in fact, it’s listed as the best-seller in Computer Monitor Arms). It provides a reasonable level of quality at a low price but fails to unseat the Workspace by Monoprice Dual Monitor Arm on our list. We’ll begin with the positives, which, to be clear, outweigh the problems. The Huanuo HNDS6 carefully walks the value tightrope to deliver a decent dual-monitor arm at a typical price of $60 (which can dip below $50 on sale). The arm’s metal construction feels rigid and looks durable. Each arm is rated to hold between 4.4 and 14.3 pounds. That’s not a lot: The Workstream by Monoprice arm is rated up to 20 pounds. Still, it’s enough to handle a huge majority of 24- and 27-inch monitors, and the monitor arms provided plenty of lift in our testing. We’re not a fan of the arm’s installation. It has two clamps instead of one unified clamp, which is strange, because the base of the monitor arm is one solid piece. There are roughly a dozen screws to install. And the included cable routing can prove hard to tighten once several cables are held within the routing. The Huanuo HNDS6 is a decent dual-monitor arm for the price and worthwhile on a discount (it was once sold for just $38). In general, though, we think the Monoprice Workstream Dual Monitor Arm provides more for a similar price. Before comparing arms, confirm your monitor uses a 75x75mm or 100x100mm VESA pattern. This VESA bolt pattern on the back of your monitor is the means by which you will attach your monitor arm. It’s rare that a monitor lacks a VESA mount, but you want to be sure. While you’re at it, also check the thickness of the desk you plan to use, since that will determine whether you need a clamp mount or grommet mount for your monitor arm/s. A thicker desk will require the latter. Purchasing a monitor arm is a bit different from purchasing most home office gear. A monitor arm, unlike a monitor, is a hefty, durable piece of equipment that never really goes obsolete. It must also support the specific functions you want out of the box, since upgrades and customization tend to be limited. If you’re still on the fence about whether a monitor arm is worth the money and the time it takes to set up, read our article that answers why a monitor arm is most definitely worth it. The range of adjustability and motion a monitor arm can offer is a critical but often overlooked feature. A monitor arm should adjust for height, tilt, swivel, and pivot—and it should do so without tools. All the monitor arms we recommend meet this standard, but some differences remain. Only some monitor arms provide 360 degrees of swivel, meaning the neck of the monitor arm can be rotated to any position. That’s handy if your desk is in the middle of your room since you can use the monitor from various positions. Most inexpensive monitor arms ditch adjustability and stick with simple tension mechanisms that are secured by a screw. It’s inexpensive but fixes the monitor’s position in place once it’s adjusted. We recommend avoiding mounts that use this strategy. None of the monitor arms tested were difficult to install, but the difference between budget and premium models was clear. Budget models require more screws to install, and the default tension of the arm’s adjustment mechanism is less likely to be suitable out-of-the-box. The ease of adjustment varies greatly, too. All the monitor arms we surveyed require an Allen wrench to adjust tension (which is necessary if the arm seems too stiff or loose), but some were much more difficult than others. The Herman Miller Flo felt smooth and effortless, while the Workstream by Monoprice required serious torque. Proper cable management is important if you value a clean, clutter-free desk. This is one aspect of design that didn’t improve with pricing. The Herman Miller Flo’s cable management was basic, while the Workstream by Monoprice hid cables well. This did come with a trade-off, though, as the Flo’s seemed least likely to cause cables to bind while moving the monitor. While cable management is useful, none of the monitor arms I tested can handle the full complement of cables that might be attached to a high-end USB-C monitor (like the Dell U3223QE). This is an aspect of monitor arm design that manufacturers could improve. It’s important to buy a monitor arm that can handle the monitor you own. This won’t be a major concern if you own a 24-inch or 27-inch monitor, as most such monitors weigh 10 pounds or less. With that said, it’s wise to double-check the monitor’s weight before buying a monitor arm. Remember the monitor’s weight can exclude its stand. Larger 32-inch, 34-inch, and 49-inch monitors are more difficult to handle and may require an upgrade to a “heavy duty” monitor arm, such as the Ergotron HX. Other things to consider with a “heavy-duty” setup are the weight, depth, and rigidity of your desk — check that the arm you are interested in is compatible with all these factors. Monitor size limits should be respected as well. It might be possible to attach a 40-inch monitor to an arm meant for a 32-inch monitor. The 40-inch monitor may even come within the arm’s weight limit. A larger monitor will distribute weight differently, however, which could cause an arm’s tension mechanism to fail. Every monitor arm we recommend was personally tested first-hand at a PC World contributor’s home or the PC World office. We examine the quality, ease of installation, and range of adjustment of each arm to verify it meets the manufacturer’s claims. The monitors we use to test arms can vary over time, but generally include at least one 27-inch and one 32-inch widescreen monitor. Monitor arms rated for “heavy duty” use were tested with at least one monitor that weighs 20 pounds or more. What is the best monitor arm? The best single monitor arm is the Ergotron LX Pro. It’s easy to set up, looks attractive, works well in day-to-day use, and, at just a little over $200, remains affordable. What is the best cheap monitor arm? The best budget monitor arm is the MSI MAG MT201. It can accommodate screens up to 49 inches and 44 pounds. There is a little bit of assembly required, but the necessary tools are supplied. But once done, adjusting the arm is easy. It also looks very nice for a budget monitor arm. MSRP is $99.99, but it’s common to see the MT201 for $70 or less. Is a monitor arm worth it? Whether a monitor arm is worth the price is subjective, but we believe our recommended monitor arms are worth making the investment. A monitor arm is easier to use than a stand, allows a wider range of adjustment, and keeps your desk clear of clutter. They’re also durable—there’s a good chance you’ll replace a monitor before the monitor arm. Are monitor arms compatible with my monitor? Nearly all monitors, and nearly all monitor arms, use the VESA mounting standard. The 100x100mm bolt pattern is by far the most common, though 75x75mm is sometimes used as an alternative. All the monitor arms we recommend support both bolt patterns. Not sure that your monitor supports VESA? Check the rear of the monitor. The VESA mount can be found in the center of the monitor, and the bolt pattern can be verified with a ruler or tape measure. This is likely beneath the neck of your monitor’s stand if you have one attached. It’s possible to mount a monitor that lacks a VESA mount, but you’ll need to purchase a VESA adapter. It’s a large, X-shaped device that clamps to the rear of the monitor. Are monitor arms compatible with my desk? Most monitor arms offer two mounting options: clamp and grommet. A clamp mount is the most common for home office use. A U-shaped clamp fits over an edge of your desk. A screw mechanism is used to secure it. Most clamps are adjusted by hand and fit a wide range of desks. It’s important to double-check a monitor arm’s specifications if your desk is more than an inch thick, as some clamp mounts are too small to work with a thick desk surface. The clamp also requires an edge that’s free of obstructions on both the top and bottom of the desk. Grommet mounts insert into the circular cut-outs found on many desks built and sold for corporate offices. A grommet mount is also a form of clamp, but size of the mechanism is different, and the mount attaches the monitor to the interior of the desk instead of an exterior edge. Nearly all monitor arms ship with a clamp and grommet mount, but grommet mounts are less common. It’s wise to double-check that a grommet mount is supported if that’s how you plan to mount the monitor arm. Will a monitor arm damage my desk? It’s possible that a monitor arm’s clamp mount, if used, will cause minor damage to your desk. It may scratch the desk’s surface when mounted or removed, and over-torquing the clamp might cause a dent on some softer desks, such as those which use a veneer over particleboard. A glass desk can also prove troublesome—refer to the desk’s manufacturer to make sure it’s safe to use a monitor arm. Do monitor arms wobble? A quality monitor arm will tame minimal monitor wobble, though some might come through if the arm is mounted to a thin, light desk. Make sure to mount the monitor arm to a secure surface and adjust the arm’s tension to a level suitable for the monitor you’ve mounted. Should I buy a $25 monitor arm on Amazon? A monitor arm’s price tag can intimidate budget shoppers. Most budget monitors sell for $200 or less. Spending another $150 to $300 for a monitor arm can seem hard to justify. Still, we encourage shoppers to avoid cheap monitor arms found on Amazon and other retailers. The least expensive monitor arms lack a dynamic tension mechanism, like a gas piston or spring. A few arms in the $35 to $50 range use a gas piston, but it’s often a wimpy example barely sufficient for holding a 27-inch monitor. Inexpensive monitor arms also lean more heavily on plastic. That’s not necessarily a problem out-of-the-box, but plastic tends to become brittle over time, which may reduce the lifespan of a monitor arm.

item.title: SALES: Arc'teryx Promo Codes & Deals November 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Whether you’re a seasoned mountaineer, a proponent of gorpcore, or a mix of both, you’re probably familiar with the Vancouver-based outdoors brand Arc’teryx (Did you know it was named after the Archaeopteryx lithographica, the first reptile to develop feathers for flight?). Famous for its waterproof Gore-Tex shell jackets, down parkas, and—if you’re a Brooklyn hipster—the iconic Bird Head Toque hat, the brand is committed to developing the very best in activewear technology, often testing its gear on the Coast Mountains of British Columbia for durability, comfort, and function. Founded in 1989 by Dave Lane as “Rock Solid,” the brand started out as a collection of climbing harnesses. After enlisting Jeremy Guard, the company was rebranded as “Arc’Teryx” in 1991, with a new logo: a stylized skeleton of the Archaeopteryx lithographica. In 1998, the brand secured a license for Gore-Tex, launching the iconic Alpha SV jacket. In the last few years, Arc’teryx has made its way into high fashion, capturing the attention of street-style icons behind the gorpcore trend and collaborating with designers like Jil Sander. While Arc’teryx gear does cost a pretty penny, there are all kinds of deals to look out for to help you save big on your next purchase. (While these discounts come directly from the brand, keep in mind outdoor outfitter REI is currently offering significant discounts on various Arc'teryx apparel). Below, find the best Arc’teryx discounts, promo codes, and offers. Arc'teryx Outlet: Save up to 50% on past season gear without a promo code Before you commit to buying something full-price, have a look at the Arc’teryx Outlet, where you can score up to 50% off a selection of men's and women’s shell jackets, base layers, and footwear—including products from Veilance, the brand’s more urban-friendly line. Men, for instance, can currently save 30% on the Solano jacket, as well as 65% on the Kragg shoe. For the steepest discounts, keep an eye out for discontinued colors and previous iterations of core products. Keep in mind, though, that all items purchased at the Arc’teryx Outlet are final sale. Part of Arc’teryx’s commitment to sustainability is ensuring products last for lifetimes. When you trade in gently used Arc’teryx gear, you’ll receive a gift card worth 30% of the original retail value. Trade-ins are processed through the Rebird Resale program—simply complete the trade-in form online to get a shipping label, then package the gear and mail it in, or drop it off in store to save on shipping fees. Only eligible items will qualify for the trade-in, so those that pose hygiene issues, like cotton T-shirts or headwear, are less likely to be accepted. A good rule of thumb is that if you wouldn’t gift it to a friend, it likely won’t be eligible. Outdoor professionals enjoy special pricing at Arc'teryx without a discount code Through Arc’teryx’s Pro Program, qualified outdoor experts and community partners—including mountain guides, park rangers, firefighters, ski instructors, and more—can take advantage of special discounted pricing. To apply, fill out an application and verify your professional credentials on the Arc’teryx site. Enjoy free standard shipping on all US orders Arc’teryx offers free shipping on all orders placed within the US—no minimum purchase required. This includes items from the Arc’teryx Outlet, and also extends to free returns within a 30-day window for most purchases. Whether you’re grabbing a pair of merino wool hiking socks or a comfortable jacket for day hikes, the price on the tag (plus tax) is all you’ll be paying. How to maximize your Arc'teryx savings for your next outdoor adventure To get the best possible deal, combine savings strategies. Use trade-in credits from the Rebird program on items already marked down in the Outlet, and check the Outlet regularly, since new styles rotate in often. Sign up for the brand newsletter to receive alerts on upcoming Arc'teryx savings opportunities.

item.title: SALES: 11 US Vacation Rentals Where the Hot Tub Comes With a View
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Travelers love to debate window vs. aisle, or whether or not a group trip is a good idea, but I’ve never met anyone who didn’t love a hot tub. It’s the amenity that separates a good vacation home from a great one—the ultimate way to wake up your system in the morning or relax tired muscles in the evening, no matter the season. The rentals on this list, from cozy log cabins in Tennessee to glassy beach houses in coastal Oregon, all promise steamy hot tubs worth planning a trip around. Whether you want to experience the stillness of the New Mexican desert, breathe in the Blue Ridge mountain air, or look out for wildlife in Texas Hill Country, you can do it all from the comfort of your very own bubbling sanctuary. For a rejuvenating weekend away, where the agenda is resetting your nervous system or simply sharing a few laughs with friends, these hot tub–included rentals in the US are just the ticket. We've selected these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews. Our top picks: Why we love it: In-unit washer/dryer, game room, outdoor spaceJust a short drive away from some of Tennessee’s best theme parks (including Dollywood), this Smoky Mountain retreat is a home the entire family will love. The 2,100-square-foot cabin is divided into three levels, each with its own bedroom (all have king-size beds) and bathroom (one has a freestanding bathtub). Kids will love the game room in the loft, as well as a few hours spent at nearby Wild Bear Falls Indoor Water Park, Anakeesta, or Ripley's Aquarium of the Smokies. After all that fun, adults can end their days in the outdoor hot tub, perfectly positioned for watching the sun set over the mountain ridge. Location: Gatlinburg, Tennessee Things to do nearby: Historic Ogle Log Cabin, Hillbilly Golf, Herbert Holt Park Why we love it: Pet-friendly, floor-to-ceiling windows, forest viewsIdeal for a couples getaway in the woods, this glassy cabin, with its soaring, floor-to-ceiling windows, is sure to provide a nature-friendly reset. It’s located just a five-minute walk away from Hocking Hills State Park and has all the modern comforts you need: a newly renovated kitchen and dining area, a queen-size bed upstairs, and, of course, an outdoor patio with a firepit and hot tub for nights spent nestled in the trees. Many reviewers gush over how spotless the place is and how close it is to hiking trails. One thing to note: AWD/4WD vehicles are recommended due to the rugged landscape. Location: Laurelville, Ohio Things to do nearby: Hocking Hills State Park, Conkles Hollow State Nature Preserve, Cedar Falls Why we love it: Game room, home gym, lake viewsThis modern masterpiece of a home, perfect for large family gatherings, was voted a 2026 Vrbo Vacation Rental of the Year. And it’s pretty easy to understand why, between the gorgeous views of Squam Lake from nearly every corner; the private dock from which to swim, kayak, or paddleboard; and the hot tub that’s built into the property. There are dozens of hiking trails nearby, whether you want to go on an easy lakeside stroll or trek to Mount Morgan. Suitable for any season, the house invites you to either laze a sunny day away on the patio’s sun chairs or curl up by the fireplace on a cooler night. item.title: SALES: 8 Dreamy Hotels Our NYC Editors Are Booking This Winter
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
If there’s one thing the editors at Condé Nast Traveler love, it’s weekendmaxxing. We’re all about scouting the very best hotels upstate, or catching a quick flight to Miami, all before returning back to our New York City office by Monday. The art of the weekend trip becomes especially important in the wintertime, when the city closes its blinds and hibernates until spring. This is when an off-season jaunt to the Rockaways, or a hideaway in a Berkshires lodge, becomes all the more appealing. Essentially, we love a trip where you can get cozy somewhere else—because sometimes all you need is a simple change of scenery to tackle the winter blues. From wellness sanctuaries nestled in the Catskills to country retreats in New England, these are the hotels our editors are eyeing for when the weather turns brisk, all within a few hours of NYC or a short flight away. - Read Full ReviewHannah Chubb, senior commerce editor Where are you staying? Mayflower Inn & Spa, Washington, Connecticut What drew you to this hotel? I visited Mayflower Inn back in spring 2024 with one of my best friends while she was pregnant with her second baby, and I’ve been dying to go back ever since. I don’t know if I’ve ever felt more relaxed than I did while there—we spent hours in the spa, chatted by the firepits, stuffed ourselves with farm-fresh meals, and feasted our eyes on some incredible interior design. What are you eating? I won’t be leaving the hotel for food, that’s for sure. I’m always impressed by the F&B at Auberge properties, and the Mayflower Inn was no exception. The Garden Room offers creative but approachable seasonal cuisine from breakfast through dinner (don’t skip the burger), and the Tap Room is where you’ll find a tavern-style food menu plus a mixologist slinging delicious cocktails and mocktails. What do you hope to get up to in the area? The Mayflower Inn is located in Washington, Connecticut, a small town in Litchfield County, a region beloved by many of my colleagues. Next time I visit the hotel, I’ll have to make a few stops along the way to see what all the fuss is about. - Read Full ReviewMadison Flager, commerce director Where are you staying? Urban Cowboy Lodge, Big Indian, New York What drew you to this hotel? Urban Cowboy Lodge has been on my weekend getaway wish list for years, and there’s something about it in winter that feels particularly charming—maybe it’s the delightful snow-filled view from the bathtub (pictured above) that drew me in. I’m imagining myself curled up with a good book by the lounge’s fireplace, draped in a Pendleton blanket, then dipping into the aforementioned copper clawfoot bathtubs. At just about two-and-a-half hours north of Manhattan, it’s a not-too-far excursion I’m saving for when I really need a break from winter in the city. What are you eating? Phoenicia Diner, of course. I’m also keen to try out some of the many craft beers at Ralph’s Bar. What do you hope to get up to in the area? I’m not a skier, so in the winter, heading to the Catskills comes with more of a stay-indoors-and-get-cozy vibe for me. Besides a pit stop at Phoenicia Diner, I imagine the furthest I’ll trek is over to the sauna and bowling alley. - Read Full ReviewJessica Chapel, commerce writer Where are you staying? The Rockaway Hotel & Spa, Rockaway Park, New York What drew you to this hotel? Aside from the ocean views—poetically perfect for New York in the winter—The Rockaway is home to one of my favorite wellness scenes in the city. The space transforms its outdoor pool area (which, in the summer months, is home to outdoor concerts and DJ-led pool parties) into the cozy Winter Pool House. The space gets decked out with outdoor cedar barrel saunas and the softest plush robes to wear while you transition to the heated outdoor pool. The warm water mixed with the ice-cold breeze coming off the nearby coastline is glorious. What are you eating? I’ll be heading to Margie’s—the mood-lit hotel lobby restaurant—and ordering a juicy cheeseburger and a frosty gin martini. What better way to warm your soul? What do you hope to get up to in the area? The beauty of visiting this hotel in winter? No summer beach crowds. I’ll likely bundle up, head to the beach for some meditation, and head right back to my cozy room at The Rockaway to soak up the views even more. - Read Full ReviewMeaghan Kenny, commerce editor Where are you staying? Wildflower Farms, Auberge Collection, Gardiner, New York What drew you to this hotel? I’ve had Wildflower Farms on my wish list for the past few years. Located in New York’s Hudson Valley, it’s a quick 90-minute drive from NYC, making it a convenient pick for couples or families seeking an easy getaway. What are you eating? I’m most eager to have coffee and pastries around the fire at the Great Porch, Wildflower’s open-air communal space with sprawling views of the Shawangunk Ridge. And of course, I’ll be dining at the resort’s on-site restaurant, Clay, where the rustic American menu is full of seasonal ingredients from local farms. What do you hope to get up to in the area? I usually try to pack as many activities and must-try coffee shops and restaurants as possible into my trip itinerary, but Wildflower Farms encourages you to slow down. You’ll find me at Thistle, the resort’s on-site spa where hand-harvested, small-batch oils and scrubs are used during tailored treatments. - Read Full ReviewArati Menon, global digital director Where are you staying? Inness, Accord, New York What drew you to this hotel? Inness is resplendent in the summer, so I’ve always been keen to see a different side of it come hunker-down weather. And if you can drag yourself out, which you should, there are loads of hikes and walks, including those along the Ashokan Reservoir, which is one of my favorite spots. What are you eating? Stacks of pancakes; comfort-food entrées like risottos; a round of Dorato Negronis at the bar. What do you hope to get up to in the area? Spending the afternoons shopping and dining in some of my favorite nearby towns, like Kingston and Woodstock. - Read Full ReviewJessica Sulima, commerce writer Where are you staying? Four Seasons Hotel at The Surf Club, Surfside, Florida What drew you to this hotel? Laze around by the pool, enjoy the quieter beaches of Surfside, and maybe stroll through the Rubell Museum in Allapattah.

item.title: SALES: Where to Eat Gluten-Free in Montreal
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Recently I’ve noticed more and more food people going to Montreal—and who can blame them? This laid-back bilingual gem on the St. Lawrence River is one of North America’s very best food cities. Personally I’ve loved it since my first visit almost 20 years ago. Montreal’s wonderful food scene draws me back year after year, sometimes multiple times,and by now the six-hour drive from my home in New York City feels like a breeze. It helps to know that my top meals of the year are waiting just across the border. But for the past two years, following my wife’s celiac diagnosis, I have been navigating the city a little differently. When I was younger, trips to Montreal meant poutine, bagels, smoked-meat sandwiches, and a plethora of other canonical Québécois favorites that happen to be full of gluten. These days we prioritize other local favorites and have developed a dependable roster of businesses we trust—and that don’t feel like a compromise. Luckily there are a ton of them; we’ve been thrilled to discover that Montreal is a paradise for gluten-free eating. In my opinion the only gluten-free Montreal-style bagels worth sampling are located in Burlington, Vermont. But Montreal is a city that takes its baked goods seriously, and it’s home to a handful of excellent dedicated gluten-free bakeries. You will not miss the bagels. Instead how about a croissant? Any gluten-free eater knows croissants are one of the hardest pastries to get right without gluten. As a rule my wife and I don’t really bother—unless we’re in Montreal. At Boulangerie Le Marquis, near Jean-Talon Market, and sister business Le Marquis Signature Santé, in Old Montreal, magnificent pains au chocolat and gluten-free croissants—available in plain, almond, and chocolate-almond varieties—arrive hot out of the oven all morning long. Flaky laminated pastry is a near-impossible feat in the gluten-free world, but Le Marquis has perfected it. We favor the pains au chocolat and almond croissants, but it’s tough to go wrong. Even more unique is the gluten-free manouché at La Bolo à Lolo, a GF market and takeaway in the Plateau. Chef and owner Gordy Moufarrej emigrated from Lebanon to Montreal as a boy and uses his mother’s homemade za’atar in these addictive flatbreads. Made from Moufarrej’s proprietary GF flour blend, they are topped with a paste of olive oil and za’atar, plus cheese if you want (you do). A number of sandwiches made with the same base are available, but we’ve never gotten past the manouché—on our last visit to Montreal, we went three days in a row. Perhaps unsurprisingly for a French-speaking city, crepes are another great option, and Montreal boasts an amazing spot for 100% buckwheat Breton-style galettes. At Crêperie du Marché, a bustling stall at Jean-Talon Market, cooks turn out a dedicated gluten-free menu of lacy galettes with both savory and sweet fillings. It’s a personal choice, but we like the cheeky selections that mix both: ham, cheese, eggs, potatoes, and a drizzle of maple syrup. Why not? Nearby is cheery, quirky Cantine Panella, a dedicated gluten-free bakery and café run by the Peruvian chef Alessandra Perona. Her South American sensibility means breads are made with flours like quinoa, cassava, and sweet potato, which gives them a delightful chewiness. We like to stock up on a few of these to bring home, though they sometimes don’t last the drive. Of all Montreal’s classic foods, rotisserie chicken might be my favorite. At Québécois-style rotisseries it’s slow-roasted on a spit and accompanied by gravy; at Portuguese spots it’s often spatchcocked and grilled over charcoal, then served with piri-piri sauce. In both cases gluten sometimes spoils the fun: Traditional establishments like the legendary Chalet Bar-B-Q and Portuguese eatery Ma Poule Mouillée both use wheat flour in their sauces. No matter—these are far from your only options. At Rôtisserie Coco Rico, a Plateau institution open since 1970, the chicken is spit-roasted and served with GF piri-piri in a mélange of the two dominant local styles. On the side fries from a dedicated GF fryer are among the city’s best (and this is a city with great french fries), but don’t sleep on the roasted potatoes, full of savory chicken flavor. More refined, and representing the French Canadian tradition, is Little Italy’s Rôtisserie La Lune, from the team behind überpopular restaurant and wine bar Mon Lapin. Gorgeous, plump birds are served with rich gluten-free gravy and excellent fries that come from a blessedly dedicated fryer. The same fryer is also responsible for the unbelievable Croqu’Ailes Farcies XL, which are deboned chicken wings stuffed with more chicken and deep-fried. Every meal here should start with these. But the kitchen has an equally deft hand with seasonal salads and veggie-focused sides—almost always gluten-free and an essential counterweight on the table. Down the street from La Lune, Mon Lapin is equally adept at catering to gluten-free diners: On two recent visits most of the menu was in play. Dishes change with the seasons, but friendly servers will guide your choices (and help you navigate the impressive wine list). Make sure to save room for the restaurant’s signature buckwheat layer cake, accented with buckwheat honey caramel, fromage blanc, and crisp shards of buckwheat tuile. I’m not sure there’s a better gluten-free dessert on the continent. Mon Lapin’s co-owners, chefs Jessica Noël and Marc-Olivier Frappier, and wine director Vanya Filipovic, are all alums of the trendsetting Little Burgundy eatery and wine bar Vin Papillon, whose chef and owner happens to be celiac. Best known as half of the duo that opened Montreal icon Joe Beef, Fred Morin now presides over those two restaurants, plus the rotisserie McKiernan and gastropub Liverpool House. His kitchens have airtight allergy protocols and are particularly sensitive to gluten-free diners because of Morin’s own celiac status. And because so many Montreal chefs have passed through Morin’s kitchens, his influence looms large over the city’s fine dining scene—and its spirit of hospitality toward those with allergies and intolerances. While all of Morin’s restaurants are fantastic, Vin Papillon is the one we come back to every year—its Jambon de la Petite-Bourgogne is one of the world’s great meat-and-cheese plates, featuring house-cured ham, the Quebec sheep-milk cheese le Fleur des Monts, and a sneaky application of brown butter that brings together all the nutty, savory notes. For dessert the restaurant often serves a gluten-free carrot cake ice cream sandwich with caramel sauce in a silver goblet. Another Joe Beef group alum, Ariel Schor, runs one of our favorite Verdun neighborhood spots with his brother, Pablo. Both natives of Argentina with Jewish roots, the Schors run a restaurant called Beba with a particular affinity for offal (organ meats) and a surprisingly light touch with creative veg dishes that change seasonally. Swiss chard leaves are stuffed with zucchini and chard stems and served with a sweet-and-sour condiment of onions, raisins, and pine nuts. Medjool dates are impishly filled with foie gras and topped with pistachio. Elsewhere on the menu expect things like tongue, rabbit, chorizo, and tripe—dishes that tend to be gluten-free. When you’re craving Gallic comfort food, Montreal overdelivers. I used to think there were Leméac people and L’Express people, that one couldn’t possibly love Montreal’s two most prominent old-school bistros equally. I was wrong. The late local architect Luc Laporte designed both dining rooms, and they each have the buzzing, joyful energy most restaurants covet. L’Express is my first love, a Montreal stalwart open since 1980 that I’ve been to more times than I can count. Its main virtues for gluten-free eaters are a dedicated fryer and incredibly good french fries—available as a stand-alone side or, even better, as part of steak frites. There are plenty of other GF mains and entrées, but room must be saved for the enormous île flottante, a classic French meringue-based dessert encased in a hardened caramel dome and surrounded by shards of candied almond. For something on the lighter side, try the unique crème brûlée with wild sweet clover from Quebec, sometimes called boreal vanilla. Leméac does not have a dedicated fryer, so fries don’t work for celiacs. But I promise you won’t miss them. We favor the textbook duck confit, served with roasted potatoes and a bright green salad. For dessert there’s an unmissable gluten-free chocolate-and-banana moelleux, a decadent cake served with caramel and popcorn ice cream, along with many other classics, including crème caramel. Montreal is also home to a number of fabulous Middle Eastern and North African restaurants, some of which can cater to gluten-free diners—albeit with asterisks. We love the standout Damas, a Syrian fine-dining spot on a pretty corner in Outremont, though gluten-free choices are limited. Still, it’s worth the trip for the ground lamb and eggplant kebab grilled over open charcoal and accompanied by charred pepper, tomato butter, and gobs of garlic labneh and the dreamy hummus topped with lamb shawarma and pine nuts, which can be served with crudités rather than pita. Both are among the best things I’ve eaten in recent memory. Le Petit Alep, a neighborhood institution near Jean-Talon, offers more Syrian and Armenian options. The marvelous mezes are largely gluten-free and served—upon request—with crudités; savory, comforting mujaddara is made with lentils and rice, no bulgur, barley, or other glutenous grains. End with the house herbal tea, a beautiful floral mixture of cardamom pods, mint, rosewater, and orange blossom. I’ve tried to make it at home, but I can’t quite replicate it. That’s okay—I’ll be back next year.

item.title: SALES: 11 Gorgeous US Ski Vacation Homes Built for Fresh Powder and Easy Slope Access
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
I’ve been skiing my entire life, venturing out for nostalgic winter weekends on the East Coast and fresh powder-chasing adventures out West. Yet somehow, the anticipation of a new ski season never gets old. Like clockwork, every winter brings a new mountain to explore, a favorite run to revisit, and plenty of reasons to start dreaming about the next snowfall. With El Niño in the conversation and ski resorts across the US gearing up for opening day, there’s no better time to get your winter plans in order. After all, a memorable ski vacation isn’t just about finding the right mountain (though I take my terrain very seriously). It’s also about the cozy ski towns, the lively après-ski scenes, the snow-covered scenery, and of course, the splendid place to retreat to when it’s time for boots to come off. When it comes to the best ski vacation homes, there are some amenities that really do take these trips to the next level: a hot tub to soothe your muscles, an in-unit washer and dryer to freshen up base layers, a nice fireplace or firepit to cozy up around, and a kitchen for easy meals at home—especially ideal after working up a big appetite on the mountain. Some of the best ski vacation rentals in the US are every bit as enticing as the mountains themselves. Think glass-walled chalets, design-forward A-frames, and tucked-away cabins with easy access to the lifts. From New England favorites to Western powder havens, these 11 standout stays are worth building your next ski or snowboard getaway around. FAQ: Which ski resorts in the US are on the Epic Pass? The Epic Pass offers skiing and snowboarding at a sprawling collection of US resorts. Major destinations include Vail, Beaver Creek, Breckenridge, Keystone, Crested Butte, Park City, Heavenly, Northstar, Kirkwood, Stevens Pass, and Stowe. There are also regional and partner resorts with more limited access, so check the specific pass tier before booking a trip. Do note that blackout dates and access limits vary by pass, so read the fine print! Which ski resorts in the US are on the Ikon Pass? The Ikon Pass has a tempting lineup as well, especially if your winter plans involve chasing snow across the Rockies and Sierras. Its US destinations include Mammoth Mountain, Palisades Tahoe, Steamboat, Winter Park, Aspen Snowmass, Copper Mountain, Big Sky, Jackson Hole, Taos Ski Valley, Deer Valley, Alta, Snowbird, and Sun Valley. Out east, you can head to Killington, Sugarbush, Stratton, Loon Mountain, Sugarloaf, or Sunday River. Where is El Niño predicted to bring snowfall this season? For the 2026-27 season, a strong El Niño is shaping the forecast, with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) expecting wetter-than-average conditions across the southern US, from California and the Southwest through the Southeast, as well as along the East Coast. This could mean more opportunities for snowfall in higher-elevation ski destinations, particularly when temperatures cooperate. However, wetter doesn't automatically mean snowier: NOAA also expects warmer-than-average conditions across much of the West and northern US Seasonal outlooks predict precipitation patterns, not specific snowfall totals, so keep an eye on shorter-range forecasts before planning a powder chase.

Source: PCMag
Search-focused AI tool Perplexity is joining rivals such as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Microsoft by introducing AI agent tech built for complex work projects. Perplexity already has a suite of agentic tools called Computer, but its new Teammates alternative is designed to build productivity-focused agents that better handle context, remember your work history, and stay accessible while working on tasks. Teammates appear in dedicated threads within Perplexity once you've created them, and each remains permanently available, able to activate at any time and work 24/7 even when you’re away from your computer. “Proactive by design, they run on automations and keep moving work forward on your behalf," Perplexity says. You can communicate with the agent in natural language and request changes at any time. If the agent asks for further information or wants to update you on its progress, it will notify you directly. The AI can also work with your other Teammate agents on complex tasks and message your real-life coworkers via Slack. The Perplexity website gives a few examples of what you can expect its agents to be able to do, including taking on roles of Ads Manager, Engineer, QA Engineer, or Legal Research Assistant. For the latter, it shows a workflow in which the agentic AI could read a contract, compare its terms with other documents, flag any problems, and then draft a response to address them.
